Title: This Week in Democracy: Courts Push Back, Congress Stirs, and Detention Conditions Boil Over
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the machinery of American government strained visibly against itself — courts checking the executive, Congress intermittently finding its footing, and a crisis in immigrant detention that grew worse by the day even as officials in New Jersey sued to gain access to the facility at its center. By Friday, the pattern was unmistakable: real institutional resistance, but resistance that remained partial, contested, and in several cases reversible.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. A federal judge ruled that the Kennedy Center could not be renamed without an act of Congress and blocked a planned two-year closure of the institution, prompting an angry, personal social-media attack on the judge from the president. The same stretch of days brought a Miami federal judge's decision to reopen a $10 billion IRS lawsuit involving Trump personally, after 35 former federal judges alleged the settlement underlying its dismissal was the product of collusion with his own Justice Department; the administration was ordered to respond by June 12 on whether the acting attorney general might need to testify. A three-judge panel that included two Trump appointees unanimously struck down Alabama's congressional map as intentionally discriminatory against Black voters, a ruling now headed toward Supreme Court review. And the Office of Management and Budget advanced a sweeping proposal — later published as a 400-page Federal Register notice — that would let political appointees cut off federal research grants that don't serve presidential priorities and would bar diversity and disparate-impact research at universities; MIT was already reporting a 20 percent decline in funding.

It was also over the weekend that the week's defining crisis began to take shape. Roughly 300 detainees at the Delaney Hall ICE facility in Newark launched a hunger and labor strike over conditions inside the facility. Guards responded with pepper spray. The Department of Homeland Security denied the strike was even happening, and the administration's border czar threatened force-feeding. By the end of the weekend, New Jersey state police had taken over from ICE at the site and clashed with protesters using tear gas and mounted officers — the first chapter in what would become a week-long standoff. Elsewhere, Trump's primary endorsement of Ken Paxton over sitting Senator John Cornyn delivered Cornyn's defeat, a vivid demonstration of the president's capacity to remove disloyal incumbents from his own party, while investigators revealed that ostensibly progressive super PACs spending heavily in Democratic primaries were secretly tied to House Republican leadership and Speaker Mike Johnson.

**Monday**

Monday brought the week's most consequential court decisions. The Supreme Court, in a 6–3 ruling, struck down the executive order denying citizenship to children born to undocumented parents, preserving the foundational 14th Amendment guarantee — though dissenting justices lent new credibility to fringe legal theories challenging the doctrine, a signal that the fight is not over. A federal judge separately blocked the administration's transfer of a national climate research supercomputing center out of Colorado, finding it likely political retaliation, while a federal appeals court ruled the Pentagon's transgender military ban likely unconstitutional and driven by animus. A Massachusetts judge blocked a Postal Service directive that would have restricted mail-ballot delivery to voters on a federal pre-approved list, protecting access in 23 states and D.C. pending appeal.

Even as courts pushed back, the administration pressed forward on other fronts. The Justice Department filed a 94-page indictment against 15 Minneapolis protesters alleging a sweeping conspiracy against ICE, without charging serious violence, while implicating groups like the AFL-CIO and DSA without formally charging them — a prosecution that read less like a response to specific criminal conduct than an effort to criminalize organizing itself. At Delaney Hall, the crisis sharpened further: ICE officers pepper-sprayed U.S. Senator Andy Kim as he attempted to visit the facility, part of a broader pattern of force against detainees and protesters that week. Reporting also surfaced that more than 100,000 immigration cases had been closed through accelerated "mega-master" hearings with high rates of in-absentia removal, and that the administration was moving to end Temporary Protected Status for more than 330,000 Haitian immigrants. The Pentagon reclassified its press office as a secure facility, requiring journalists to schedule appointments to speak with officials — another increment in a long pattern of tightening access during an active conflict. And after his preferred candidate trailed in California's gubernatorial primary, Trump ordered the Justice Department to investigate the state's elections based on unsubstantiated fraud claims.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday centered on money and war powers. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told a House panel the Justice Department would abandon the $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund — widely criticized as a vehicle for rewarding Trump allies and January 6 defendants — though he declined to commit the reversal in writing, and the administration preserved a separate IRS audit immunity arrangement. House Republicans moved to formally kill the fund and separately blocked $1 billion in security funding for Trump's White House ballroom project, both rebukes from within his own party. Speaker Johnson, meanwhile, had sent members home a day early before the holiday specifically to prevent a floor vote on a war-powers resolution concerning Iran — a deliberate maneuver to avoid a constitutional check on war-making. Trump signed an executive order directing the seizure of bank accounts and assets tied to undocumented immigrants, framed as a response to anti-ICE unrest. In New Jersey, state and local officials sued the private operator of Delaney Hall, Geo Group, after being denied health-inspector access to the facility; DHS called the lawsuits frivolous. And Trump explicitly tied federal funding to his endorsement of a California gubernatorial candidate, telling voters that money "will flow" based on his preference — a direct and open form of coercive leverage.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday was arguably the week's most consequential single day for the structure of federal governance. Trump signed an executive order, paired with a "Schedule Policy/Career" reclassification, stripping adverse-action protections from roughly 8,000 to 10,000 senior federal policy positions, enabling at-will removal of civil servants deemed insufficiently aligned with presidential priorities — a direct threat to the merit-based character of federal administration. Hours later, the House passed a war-powers resolution directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran absent congressional authorization, 215–208, with four Republicans joining Democrats — the first such measure to succeed after months of blocked attempts. The House also advanced a Ukraine aid package providing $8 billion in loans and $300 million in security assistance, 218–204, over leadership's apparent objections, and the Senate parliamentarian's ruling forced Senate Republicans to formally strip the ballroom security funding from a reconciliation bill. Trump also signed a sweeping customs enforcement order overhauling importer-of-record regulations and expanding executive authority over trade enforcement. At Delaney Hall, the standoff escalated again: federal agents used force against detainees and protesters, pepper-spraying Senator Kim and demonstrators once more, while the administration's border czar threatened to send "tactical units" into New Jersey. On a quieter note, Kennedy Center staff began switching signage back to the institution's original name, the first visible sign of compliance with the court order against its attempted rebranding.

**Thursday**

By Thursday, the House had repassed its war-powers resolution 215–208 and the Ukraine Support Act 226–195, with 18 Republicans defying Speaker Johnson — though a presidential veto remained likely and the measures' practical force uncertain. The Senate, meanwhile, narrowly rejected an amendment to permanently bar the anti-weaponization fund, 49–50, with three Republicans crossing party lines in support but falling one vote short. A *Washington Post* investigation found that fourteen of 27 known corporate donors to Trump's $400 million ballroom project had received new or expanded federal contracts worth over $50 billion, including major new Lockheed Martin awards — a pattern suggesting a direct relationship between private donations to a presidential project and the award of lucrative federal business. The human cost of the detention crisis also became starkly visible: a 43-year-old detainee with no criminal record died in ICE custody at a Louisiana facility despite prior federal inspection warnings, the 50th such death under this administration, while separate reporting documented migrant children re-separated from their families despite a binding legal settlement, and ICE rescinded its requirement to report in-custody deaths within 30 days of release. New Jersey's governor announced a $12 million increase in funding for immigrants' legal defense, a remedial response to mounting public pressure. Elsewhere, U.S. crude and strategic petroleum reserves fell to their lowest levels in roughly two decades as the administration drew down reserves to offset Iran-war-driven price spikes, and the administration began dismantling a $368 million deep-ocean climate observation system.

**Friday**

The week closed with the Senate's passage, 52–47, of a $70 billion immigration enforcement package funding ICE and Border Patrol through the end of the president's term — achieved through budget reconciliation specifically to bypass a filibuster, and containing no guardrails on the anti-weaponization fund whose future had seemed uncertain just days earlier. Trump signed a national security memorandum directing rapid adoption of artificial intelligence across military and intelligence operations, establishing new computing infrastructure with limited specified independent oversight. Courts delivered more rebukes: a federal judge issued a 135-page ruling striking down an immigration freeze affecting 39 countries as driven by unlawful animus and ordered the administration to restart halted asylum processing. Yet the detention crisis showed no sign of resolution — detainees at a Florida facility reported guards withholding food and water to coerce signatures on documents they could not read, children at a Texas facility were served food containing live worms and mold, and ICE formally rescinded its 30-day death-reporting requirement. The Justice Department sent a federal prosecutor to observe ballot processing in Los Angeles County as Trump continued pressing unsubstantiated fraud claims about the California primary. And in an unusual breach of diplomatic norms, the State Department and Vice President JD Vance invoked a British murder case to promote messaging about "civilizational decline," intervening directly in an allied nation's domestic politics.

Taken as a whole, the week illustrated both the resilience and the fragility of institutional checks under sustained pressure. Courts intervened repeatedly and substantively — on birthright citizenship, climate research retaliation, transgender service members, mail ballots, and an immigration freeze — yet the administration continued to contest whether judicial review should apply to some of its actions at all. Congress found rare bipartisan footing on war powers and briefly forced the retreat of a widely criticized spending fund, but could not convert either into a durable, veto-proof outcome. And at Delaney Hall, the clash between detainees seeking basic humane treatment and state and federal authorities deploying force against them, even as elected officials tried to assert oversight, stood as the week's starkest reminder that institutional pushback, however real, has not yet been enough to stop documented harm from accumulating on the ground. ```
Excerpt: This week showed a pattern increasingly familiar in this administration: aggressive executive assertions of power met by institutional pushback that was real but incomplete.

Title: The Week the Checks Pushed Back
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the executive branch tested nearly every boundary available to it, and the institutions built to resist that testing—mostly courts, occasionally Congress—pushed back with unusual force. By week's end, judges had struck down a visa tax, ordered the president's name off a federally chartered arts center, and shielded the Federal Reserve chair from retaliatory subpoenas, even as Congress delivered the administration $70 billion in unconditional immigration enforcement money in the same stretch that a major surveillance law was allowed to lapse over a personnel dispute. Overseas, policy toward Iran swung from announced airstrikes to a disputed ceasefire within days. At home, a New Jersey detention facility became the site of a hunger strike met with tear gas, and a television correspondent with 37 years at his network lost his job for refusing to shade the news in the government's favor.

**The Weekend**

The country was still absorbing an active military confrontation with Iran as the weekend opened, even as the president's public attention seemed to drift elsewhere. While Iranian missiles and drones struck American military facilities, Trump posted self-promotional videos and aired grievances about golf course landscaping at Joint Base Andrews; a clip appeared to show him dozing at his desk during an official signing, prompting widespread mockery. That same weekend, he sat for a combative interview with NBC's Kristen Welker, who pressed him for evidence behind his claims that the 2020 election and a recent California election had been rigged. He called her "crooked or stupid," unclipped his microphone, and left early.

In France, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth used a D-Day commemoration to describe European immigration as an "invasion," language borrowed directly from white nationalist rhetoric that strained relationships with allied governments at a ceremony meant to honor a shared military sacrifice. Away from the cameras, ICE denied Senator Andy Kim access to speak with detainees during an oversight visit to the Delaney Hall facility in Newark, where he witnessed a detainee in apparent medical distress and received no information about her condition — at a facility with a single full-time doctor for hundreds held there. And in a federal courtroom, a Justice Department attorney argued that courts had no authority to review the administration's demolition of the White House's East Wing, a position that, pressed to its logical end, would place even the Statue of Liberty beyond judicial reach.

**Monday**

The courts began answering back. A federal judge in Massachusetts struck down Trump's $100,000 supplemental fee on H-1B visa petitions, ruling it an unlawful tax that only Congress could impose and calling the administration's justification "cursory." The same day, a different judge ordered Trump's name removed from the Kennedy Center, finding that only Congress had authority to rename the institution, and temporarily halted a quarter-billion-dollar renovation. The Center complied by scrubbing the name from its website ahead of a Friday deadline — though the larger fight over physical compliance was only beginning.

Monday also brought troubling revelations from inside network news: fired CBS correspondent Scott Pelley alleged that news director Bari Weiss had pressured him to misrepresent anti-ICE protesters as more violent than they were and to distort a shooting victim's story to match the administration's preferred account. He said the pressure was unlike anything in his career, and that he was dismissed after refusing to comply.

Elsewhere, Vice President Vance announced he would refer Minnesota's governor and attorney general to the Justice Department over unsubstantiated claims of fraud tied to Somali immigrants, a move both officials dismissed as political retaliation against a Democratic-led state. Trump, meanwhile, demanded that Senate Majority Leader Thune fire the chamber's nonpartisan parliamentarian after she ruled that a voter-restriction bill could not ride through budget reconciliation, while border czar Tom Homan announced plans for an ICE surge in New York explicitly tied to the state's sanctuary legislation. The day closed with Trump attending an NBA Finals game at Madison Square Garden under an extraordinary security footprint that closed streets and canceled public watch parties, only to be greeted with loud boos from the crowd.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday's developments centered on congressional oversight and personnel. House Oversight Chair James Comer declined a Republican colleague's request to subpoena Todd Blanche over the Epstein files, a refusal Democrats characterized as enabling a cover-up. That same day, Trump formally nominated Blanche — his former personal defense attorney, who as acting Attorney General had pursued cases against Trump's perceived enemies and backed a $1.8 billion discretionary fund — to lead the Justice Department permanently.

In a separate and consequential move, Trump accelerated the departure of Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard and announced that Bill Pulte, the head of the Federal Housing Finance Agency with no intelligence background, would take over as acting DNI. The decision triggered immediate bipartisan alarm in the Senate, given a looming deadline to reauthorize a major surveillance authority — a fight that would come to a head by week's end. Elsewhere, Bill Gates answered closed-door questions from House Oversight about his past contacts with Jeffrey Epstein, and the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued an opinion concluding that longstanding federal guidelines for proving workplace discrimination were unconstitutional, raising the bar for future claims.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday brought one of the week's defining legislative moments. After eighteen hours of debate in which Senate Republicans blocked Democratic amendments targeting the administration's discretionary spending fund, ballroom expenditures, and leadership conflicts at DHS, the House passed the Secure America Act by a two-vote margin, and Trump signed it into law. The bill ended a 75-day Department of Homeland Security shutdown and locked in $70 billion in unrestricted funding for ICE and Customs and Border Protection through the end of Trump's term — money delivered without the accountability conditions Democrats had sought for an agency with a documented record of deaths in custody. The same day, Trump pressed Congress to simultaneously pass a $350 billion military spending increase and the SAVE America Act, a bill requiring proof-of-citizenship for voting and restricting mail-in ballots, attempting to move both through reconciliation and splitting his own party over the maneuver.

Investigative reporting added further texture to the week. ProPublica detailed how a $100 million investment from an Indian billionaire into a company tied to Donald Trump Jr. coincided with sanctions relief and tariff exemptions, while Reuters found the Trump family had earned $2.3 billion from cryptocurrency licensing since the term began, with over a million investors suffering losses, and that a pharmaceutical executive facing FDA enforcement had donated $1 million to Trump's political operation during the agency's response window. Separately, reporters uncovered that betting platforms Polymarket and Kalshi had sponsored influencers spreading false claims about a rigged Los Angeles mayoral race, and that the dark-money group One Nation was running fabricated local news sites across six Senate battleground states.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the week's most volatile day on the international front. Trump posted that the United States would strike Iran "VERY HARD TONIGHT," floating the seizure of Kharg Island and Iran's oil infrastructure in terms reminiscent of the earlier seizure of Venezuelan oil assets. Hours later, he announced the strikes were off, claiming a deal had been reached and endorsed by multiple regional governments — an account that Israeli officials and Iranian state media immediately disputed. The reversal left the actual state of American policy toward Iran unresolved heading into the weekend.

That same day, the fight over intelligence leadership came to a head: the House failed to extend FISA Section 702 in a 218-198 vote, as Democrats and a number of Republicans withheld support in protest of Pulte's planned elevation to acting DNI. Trump then withdrew the Pulte nomination in favor of Jay Clayton, who likewise lacked intelligence experience, setting up a rushed confirmation process even as the surveillance authority lapsed with Fourth Amendment questions about ongoing collection left unaddressed.

Elsewhere, roughly 100 FBI agents raided the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter-registration nonprofit serving historically disenfranchised communities, seizing devices and visiting staff members' homes under a warrant citing fraud concerns that statistical evidence does not support. Federal prosecutors also unsealed an indictment against eight pro-Palestinian activists accused of running an intimidation campaign against University of Michigan officials, and DHS issued a waiver suspending environmental and historic-preservation law to permit border wall construction through Big Bend National Park, an area accounting for a fraction of one percent of unauthorized crossings nationwide. A federal judge, meanwhile, acquitted former New York City comptroller Brad Lander of obstruction charges stemming from his protest at an ICE facility, crediting his account over the government's. Economic warning signs surfaced as well: oil executives privately told the White House that gasoline could reach five dollars a gallon, with strategic reserves near 1983-era lows, while wholesale inflation climbed to its highest annual rate since 2022.

**Friday**

Friday brought the week's reckonings to their sharpest points. The Kennedy Center's board, facing the court-ordered deadline to remove Trump's name, amended its bylaws hours beforehand to claim that compliance would trigger a requirement to return every donation received since Trump had taken control of the institution — a maneuver legal experts described as a textbook breach of fiduciary duty designed to hold the board itself hostage. The D.C. Circuit denied an emergency stay, Judge Cooper separately rejected a similar request from the Justice Department, and workers removed the lettering from the building's facade that evening, after the department had asked for extra time specifically to avoid public visibility of the compliance.

The same day, it emerged that the administration had redirected $352 million in Secret Service funding toward the White House ballroom project, after Congress had explicitly declined to appropriate $1 billion for it — a reversal of Trump's repeated public promise that the project would be entirely privately financed. Trump also pushed Congress to pass a symbolic resolution "expunging" both of his impeachments, a gesture with no legal effect but clear historical intent.

At Delaney Hall, the standoff over detention conditions escalated sharply: nearly forty women began a hunger and labor strike, joining more than 300 men who had been striking since late May, while New Jersey and Newark police deployed tear gas against supporters outside the facility and arrested dozens. ICE and the private contractor Geo Group responded by canceling visitation and transferring roughly ninety detainees, even as the Department of Homeland Security publicly denied the strike was occurring at all.

On the Iran front, state media in Tehran published what it described as draft terms of a new agreement, including a $300 billion reconstruction package, which the White House disputed; Trump called Iran's account "weak and pathetic" while making unverified claims of his own about extracting Iranian oil during the conflict.

Courts remained active through the week's final day as well: Judge Brinkema extended her injunction against the administration's $1.8 billion discretionary fund, requiring sworn declarations from senior officials that it would not proceed, while Judge Boasberg declined to lift his order shielding Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell from subpoenas he found were politically motivated.

**Taken as a whole**

The week showed an unusually direct contest between an executive branch willing to test nearly every limit on its authority and the narrower set of institutions still capable of enforcing one. Courts did the heaviest lifting — vacating an unlawful tax, defending a statutorily named cultural institution against a board's own resistance, and shielding a central bank chair from prosecutorial pressure — while Congress proved more uneven, delivering vast enforcement funding with no strings attached in the same week it allowed a major surveillance law to expire over a dispute about personnel qualifications. Abroad, the handling of the Iran crisis moved by presidential announcement and reversal rather than through any visible deliberative process, leaving allies and adversaries alike uncertain which version of American policy to credit. And within the country's own borders, the treatment of detained immigrants, a fired journalist, and a raided voter-registration group pointed to a pattern in which dissent and oversight met resistance rather than response. Historians of this period are likely to note not any single event but the recurrence: courts ruling, the executive complying slowly or defiantly, and the public left to judge, week after week, how much the compliance was worth. ```
Excerpt: This was a week defined by friction between an executive branch testing the outer limits of its authority and institutions—mostly courts, occasionally Congress—pushing back.

Title: A Birthday Party, a Vanishing War Rationale, and an Expanding Enforcement State
Content:
```markdown This was a week that began with a party and ended with a war's rationale quietly discarded, and in between, the machinery of government bent repeatedly toward personal interest, secrecy, and selective enforcement — even as courts and some state actors pushed back hard enough to leave marks.

The weekend set the tone. Trump turned the White House South Lawn into the site of a commercial UFC fight card to mark his 80th birthday, an event bankrolled in part by federal agencies and sponsored by his family's cryptocurrency venture. Courts declined to intervene despite challenges alleging misuse of public resources and conflicts tied to his financial stake in UFC's parent company. Military ceremonial units were deployed for an associated press event, and when a fighter used the platform to spread a racist, sexist conspiracy theory about Michelle Obama, Trump offered no rebuke. The spectacle sat alongside a more sobering set of judicial actions: after emergency appeals failed, workers removed Trump's name from the Kennedy Center facade under court order, and a separate federal judge ordered restoration of slavery, civil rights, and Indigenous history displays that had been stripped from national parks under an earlier executive order. Both rulings reaffirmed that courts, not unilateral executive will, still governed how public institutions were named and how public history was told. That same weekend, Trump signed a sweeping, multi-year DHS funding package expanding immigration enforcement without new oversight measures, even as a federal judge blocked a separate $1.8 billion fund that could have compensated Trump allies, including January 6 defendants, as supposed victims of government "weaponization." And in a reversal that would define the week's second half, Trump declared, on his birthday, that the conflict with Iran was over, authorizing reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and thanking Russia and China for their help — a declaration whose terms Iranian officials would later describe very differently.

By Monday, several of these threads had already hardened. Reporting revealed the administration had seriously weighed suspending habeas corpus to speed deportations after the Supreme Court affirmed migrants' right to challenge removals in court — a measure the Constitution reserves for rebellion or invasion. Governor Gavin Newsom announced that Trump had directed Justice Department investigations into him and his wife, with agents contacting associates and demanding records in what Newsom called a political fishing expedition aimed at a likely 2028 rival. The FBI, meanwhile, disrupted a genuine threat, arresting five men across four states in an alleged plot to attack the UFC event with explosive-laden drones and snipers — a reminder that law enforcement's protective function persisted even as other parts of the administration strained public trust. That strain deepened with allegations that FBI Director Kash Patel had diverted more than a million dollars in bonuses to loyalist agents, and with the administration's continued refusal to release the actual text of the Iran memorandum even while insisting a deal was "complete." Locally, Shasta County voters approved a measure gutting mail-in and early voting in favor of hand counts, prompting California's attorney general to announce a lawsuit arguing counties cannot unilaterally override statewide election law.

Tuesday brought the week's gravest civil-liberties confrontation. Federal agents shot and killed two civilians, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, during immigration enforcement operations in Minnesota. No charges followed. Instead, officials including Stephen Miller and JD Vance reportedly pushed to invoke the Insurrection Act against the protests that erupted in response, while federal prosecutors charged fifteen people with conspiracy over the demonstrations themselves. The asymmetry was stark: lethal force against civilians drew no prosecution, while protest of that force drew prosecution and talk of military suppression. The same day, the Kennedy Center's Trump-appointed board missed its court-ordered deadline to remove his name by twelve hours, then complied only grudgingly, covering the facade with a tarp — a small but telling display of institutional resistance even in defeat. Patel's troubles widened further when he posted details of the sealed UFC-attack investigation on social media, apparently for personal credit, prompting House Judiciary Democrats to formally investigate both that disclosure and the bonus allegations. Elsewhere, the week's recurring symbol of mismanagement took shape: a $14 million no-bid renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, awarded to a firm with ties to Trump's golf properties, produced a severe algae bloom within days of completion, prompting conservative media to falsely blame sabotage while workers dumped hydrogen peroxide into the water. Meanwhile, the Iran story deepened considerably: the administration released $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets and granted access to $300 billion more for reconstruction, with analysts warning the deal's vague language effectively ceded Iran control over the Strait of Hormuz — a cession Iran would soon assert by charging transit fees. When Senator Lindsey Graham voiced skepticism about the deal, Trump told reporters Graham would be "in big trouble" if he didn't fall in line, an explicit threat against a sitting senator over a policy disagreement. Separately, internal documents showed the White House ballroom project's cost had ballooned from a promised $200 million to roughly $600 million, more than half of it taxpayer-funded, directly contradicting Trump's earlier claim that no public money was involved. And Trump announced he would keep a Qatari-donated jet as a personal aircraft after leaving office, while the acting Labor Secretary threatened to withhold unemployment insurance funds from Democratic-led states over unsubstantiated fraud claims.

Wednesday brought formal resolution, of a sort, to the Iran question. Trump signed the memorandum of understanding at Versailles, reversing an earlier plan to let Vance sign in his place. A government official read reporters the agreement's fourteen points, confirming sanctions relief, the $300 billion reconstruction fund, and nuclear language that echoed the 2015 deal Trump had once torn up. Republican senators, including Cassidy, Cruz, and Tillis, publicly condemned the agreement as a capitulation, exposing a real rift within the president's own party over both the deal's substance and the secrecy surrounding it. The same day, Reuters reported that deaths in ICE custody had more than doubled under the administration, even as federal prosecutors in Minnesota dropped eighteen of thirty-six cases against immigration-enforcement protesters after a judge found one charging document to be a "false affidavit" — though new charges were filed against others in the same breath. Reporting also catalogued a broader, multi-state pattern of local voting restrictions, from photo ID requirements to drop-box removals to certification refusals, stretching from Huntington Beach to Wausau, with courts intervening in several instances. Convicted January 6 defendants filed federal tort claims seeking compensation, drawing on the same judgment fund that had powered the now-blocked "anti-weaponization" fund, following earlier DOJ settlements with Michael Flynn and Carter Page. DHS announced it would begin relocating detainees from the Alligator Alcatraz facility, citing hurricane season, though advocacy groups remained skeptical and continued pursuing permanent closure through litigation. And hours before a scheduled Senate hearing, Trump abruptly cancelled the confirmation process for a permanent Director of National Intelligence, ensuring a loyalist remained in the acting role and bypassing a core constitutional check on appointments.

Thursday delivered the week's sharpest reversal. At the G7, Trump dismissed the enriched-uranium removal he had once called his war's central objective, calling it "irrelevant," and praised Iran's leadership as rational and non-radicalized — a striking turnaround from his earlier calls for regime change, offered without explanation for what had actually been won or why the war had been fought. Not every pressure point that day bent toward the administration's wishes, though: Georgia's House Speaker announced Republicans would not redraw the state's congressional map despite Trump's urging to exploit a Supreme Court ruling that had weakened Voting Rights Act protections, citing the need for a deliberate process and organized Democratic opposition. Elsewhere, the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel issued a memo arguing that federal disability law does not require community-based care alternatives to institutionalization, explicitly breaking with three decades of courts' understanding of the Olmstead precedent. House Democrats demanded Epstein-related records from Harvard and Bard College over their historical ties to the convicted trafficker. And in a small, almost absurd coda to the ongoing pool saga, a 67-year-old former Olympic canoe racer was arrested for misdemeanor destruction of government property after reaching into the Reflecting Pool to feel its peeling epoxy coating. The administration also moved to sharply accelerate denaturalization proceedings, with CNN reporting plans for at least 250 cases by October, compared with only 166 over the previous eighteen years combined.

The week closed on Friday with the Iran deal still being sold as triumph even as its costs mounted elsewhere. The White House published a fact sheet promoting the memorandum as a historic achievement, even as reporting revealed officials had delayed for months the release of a government report on voting-machine vulnerabilities ahead of the midterms, reportedly out of concern the incoming acting intelligence director would instead chase unfounded fraud claims. A federal judge found that immigration officials had likely detained Salah Sarsour, a Wisconsin mosque president and legal permanent resident, in retaliation for his Palestinian rights advocacy, after Secretary of State Rubio personally signed a memo declaring him deportable — a ruling that reaffirmed First Amendment limits on enforcement power even as other prosecutions continued. The RNC chair falsely claimed the UFC event had outdrawn the Super Bowl by more than a hundred million viewers, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni publicly denounced Trump for fabricating details of their G7 meeting, prompting Italy to cancel a planned diplomatic visit. DHS canceled its plan to convert a Georgia warehouse, purchased for $128 million, into a 10,000-bed detention facility, following sustained local opposition and litigation. North Carolina's legislature advanced bills that Black city council members said were designed to dilute their electoral power, over Governor Stein's public objection. Federal investigators who had infiltrated encrypted Signal chats used by Minneapolis protesters secured conspiracy indictments against fifteen people. And a proposed one-time wealth tax on billionaires qualified for California's November ballot despite tens of millions of dollars spent against it by some of the very billionaires it would tax.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a government pulling in several directions at once. Spectacle and self-interest were braided through public institutions, from the lawn to the ballroom to the reflecting pool. A war was announced, signed, and then stripped of its own justification within days, its terms disputed by the very foreign government it concerned. Lethal force against civilians went unanswered while protest of that force drew prosecution, and a mosque leader's detention was found to be retaliation for protected speech. Yet courts intervened to restore erased history and enforce a renaming order; a state legislature refused to exploit a weakened voting-rights ruling; and sustained local opposition halted a major detention facility before it opened. None of these counterweights undid the week's central pattern, but they marked, clearly, that the pattern was still being contested — in courtrooms, in statehouses, and in the gap between what officials claimed and what the record showed. ```
Excerpt: This week fused spectacle, secrecy, and institutional friction.

Title: A Reflecting Pool, a Supreme Court Reversal, and a Housing Bill Held Hostage
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which a government agency could not keep a swimming pool clean, and the Supreme Court dismantled a precedent that had governed the presidency since 1935. Both stories ran in parallel for seven days, one absurd and one structural, and by Friday it was clear they belonged to the same account of how power was being exercised. Courts pushed back harder than almost any other institution, immigration protections for hundreds of thousands of people were finally and permanently stripped away, nine protesters were sentenced to decades in prison, and a bipartisan vote to limit a war collapsed within forty-eight hours under direct presidential pressure.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone with a pair of Supreme Court rulings that would come to define the week's second half. In twin 6-3 decisions, the Court allowed the administration to terminate Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitians and several thousand Syrians, and separately cleared the way for asylum seekers to be physically turned back at the border. Both rulings arrived despite Trump's documented disparaging remarks about the countries in question, and both would be finalized later in the week with no further avenue for judicial review.

Alongside that, a cluster of federal courts pushed in the opposite direction on enforcement tactics. A judge ordered the release of a religious leader detained for pro-Palestinian speech; another barred most ICE courthouse arrests in New York; a Trump-appointed judge called ICE practices "abhorrent and illegal"; and Human Rights Watch documented unlawful killings and roughly 4,000 detentions tied to a Minnesota operation, where a separate investigation found that 93 percent of street arrests in New York and New Jersey targeted Latinos. The weekend also saw the Justice Department indict 15 Minnesota protest defendants while publicly emphasizing alleged Antifa ties — a framing that would matter more by midweek — and Trump installed William Pulte, a political loyalist with no intelligence background, as acting director of national intelligence. Within a day, Pulte ordered roughly 300 firings at the National Counterterrorism Center.

It was also over the weekend that the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool first became a national story, as Trump began blaming unspecified "vandals" for algae and peeling coating that were, by all available evidence, the product of a botched $14.2 million renovation.

**Monday**

The administration's foreign policy took an abrupt turn. The Treasury Department issued a 60-day license permitting Iranian oil sales in U.S. dollars, following Vice President Vance's announcement of a nuclear inspections agreement reached at a Switzerland summit. Iran almost immediately and publicly disputed the terms Vance had described, particularly around inspector access, leaving a major sanctions reversal resting on a diplomatic claim the other side denied.

The Justice Department also sued New York over its laws barring masked federal enforcement and local cooperation agreements with ICE, while New York filed its own suit over the administration's noncompliance — a dispute over the basic boundary between state and federal authority. Public health policy absorbed further cuts: NIH froze HIV research funding in South Africa, a proposed 2027 budget would eliminate the CDC's HIV-prevention budget entirely, and the House proposed stripping $225 million from the Ryan White program, compounding new Medicaid work requirements that threaten coverage for millions. Trump also renewed his push for a National Guard deployment in Chicago over Governor Pritzker's objections.

Quietly, FEC filings revealed a Republican dark-money network funneling more than $4.3 million into ostensibly progressive PACs designed to boost weaker Democratic primary candidates, while AI industry super PACs spent over $24 million to influence a single New York primary centered on AI regulation — a story that would resolve later in the week.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the sharpest split of the week between judicial restraint and executive escalation. Federal courts blocked the use of a flawed immigration database to purge voter rolls, ruled against the Justice Department in its ninth consecutive voter-file case, quashed subpoenas against Minnesota officials as politically motivated, and saw the Seventh Circuit order DOJ to slow its voter-roll actions in Wisconsin — a near-total judicial rebuff of the administration's effort to centralize control over state voter data ahead of the midterms.

At the same time, nine Texas protesters convicted after a 2025 demonstration at an ICE detention center were sentenced to between 30 and 100 years, including one defendant who had not even been present at the protest. It was the first case to apply Trump's "antifa" domestic terrorism declaration, and the sentences exceeded those handed down for January 6 defendants — an unprecedented use of terrorism statutes against political dissent.

Trump also turned on the press that day, calling New York Times reporters "corrupt and unethical cowards" and their Iran war coverage "TREASONOUS" after a story questioned the war's achievements, announcing he would fold the reporting into an existing lawsuit against the paper. Separately, the Justice Department opened a civil rights investigation into a Brooklyn coffee shop that had briefly banned a pro-Israel congressman, raising its own questions about using federal power against ordinary political speech.

The reflecting pool story escalated in parallel: an Olympic canoeist was arrested for touching the peeling liner, National Guard troops and out-of-state police patrolled the site, and Trump threatened ten-year prison sentences while repeating unsubstantiated damage claims. And in a genuine break from the week's pattern, the Senate passed a war-powers resolution requiring congressional authorization for continued Iran military action, 50-48, with four Republicans joining Democrats — the first time such a measure had cleared both chambers.

**Wednesday**

That bipartisan moment did not survive contact with the president. Trump confronted Senators Cassidy and others at a Capitol lunch, accusing them of disloyalty over the war-powers vote; Cassidy said he matched the president's raised volume.

The same day delivered the week's most consequential single ruling: in Trump v. Slaughter, the Supreme Court overturned Humphrey's Executor, the 1935 precedent that had protected independent agency leaders from removal without cause, following Trump's earlier firing of FTC Commissioner Rebecca Slaughter. Legal experts warned the decision effectively installs a loyalty test for agency leadership across the federal government. The Court also ruled that border officials may deport lawful permanent residents suspected of crimes of "moral turpitude" without the clear-and-convincing evidence previously required, stripping an established due-process safeguard from green-card holders.

Appeals courts continued resisting the administration's voter-roll efforts — the Sixth Circuit rejected a DOJ suit against Michigan — extending an unbroken losing streak across 30 states and the District of Columbia. And the Texas protester sentences were finalized in full: eight defendants received 50 to 100 years and a ninth received 30 years for possessing political materials, with legal experts calling the outcome a direct attack on protest and ideological expression. Separately, ICE and CBP surveillance contract spending reached a record $513 million, and the $24 million tech-industry fight over New York's 12th district primary concluded with the AI-safety-aligned candidate's defeat.

**Thursday**

By Thursday, the war-powers resolution had collapsed entirely. After Trump called Cassidy a "lunatic" and summoned him to a White House briefing, the Senate reversed itself, voting 50-47 against the same measure it had passed two days earlier — a bipartisan check on war powers dismantled within 48 hours through direct presidential pressure on individual senators.

Congress absorbed a second blow to its independence the same day: minutes before a scheduled signing ceremony, Trump canceled his signature on a bipartisan housing bill that had passed 85-5 in the Senate and 358-32 in the House, demanding the Senate first pass the SAVE Act, a voting-restriction measure. He separately conditioned renewal of FISA surveillance authority on the same demand, prompting Rep. Luna to shut down the House floor and triggering a 19-day Senate adjournment.

Courts, meanwhile, kept striking at the underlying premise of those demands: Judge Casper permanently blocked the administration's proof-of-citizenship voter registration order, and Judge Talwani ruled unconstitutional an executive order tying mail-ballot delivery to federal voter-roll submission, both finding that the Constitution grants the president no specific authority over elections.

The Supreme Court's TPS and asylum rulings were finalized the same day in Mullin v. Doe and related cases, barring judicial review of the TPS terminations and upholding the border "metering" policy; Justice Kagan's dissent described the president's statements about the affected countries as "repellent and racially inflected." Judges also kept pressing the administration on transparency, ordering further disclosure in the Epstein files matter and demanding explanation for a tarp obscuring the Kennedy Center facade after a court-ordered name change.

Away from the courts, Trump commissioned a 250-foot triumphal arch he said would be privately funded, even as a New York Times analysis found his 18 major second-term construction projects carried more than $1 billion in potential taxpayer cost. He also announced on social media that he had directed the Justice Department to investigate oil companies over gas prices. In California, a one-time 5 percent billionaire wealth tax qualified for the November ballot after gathering double the required signatures, prompting tech billionaires to begin funding competing measures to block it. And Senator Wyden warned that HHS was preparing to deport more than 500 unaccompanied migrant children using a legal framework without statutory authority, ahead of a June 30 court deadline.

**Friday**

The week closed with the TPS and asylum rulings fully in effect and the administration treating them as a political victory: a White House fact sheet celebrated the decisions and listed 60 immigration enforcement actions as the "largest and most aggressive" crackdown in American history, even as advocates warned the Court's reasoning put 1.3 million people across more than a dozen TPS-covered countries at risk.

Trump, addressing the Faith & Freedom Coalition, called Democratic opponents "godless communists" and "animals" following a wave of progressive primary wins, falsely linking them to violent communism; Speaker Johnson echoed the rhetoric and separately pledged to shield the administration from oversight if Republicans retained Congress in the midterms. White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller stated plainly that the country "doesn't have a future" without ending birthright citizenship, an explicit statement of intent to dismantle a 14th Amendment guarantee.

Civil liberties concerns deepened further: at least half of roughly 90 people arrested protesting an ICE detention center in New Jersey were contacted by FBI agents seeking to recruit them as informants, and Justice Department data showed that 57 percent of more than 750,000 children facing deportation hearings lacked legal representation — a higher rate than for unrepresented adults. In smaller but telling episodes, an anonymous, fabricated child-abuse report briefly separated former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg's family, and Representative Tom Emmer told a political audience that Somalis "don't assimilate" and should "go the hell back," a sharp reversal from his earlier public praise of Somali immigrants.

**Through the Week**

Threaded through all six days was the reflecting pool, which never stopped being both ridiculous and revealing. A government contractor's failure became, in the president's telling, a conspiracy of leftist saboteurs; an elderly Olympic canoeist was detained for touching the pool's peeling liner; out-of-state police and National Guard troops patrolled a public monument against a threat no evidence supported; and the National Park Service ultimately awarded at least $1.7 million in repair work without competitive bidding to a company owned by a major Trump donor. None of this rose to the constitutional stakes of the week's Supreme Court rulings, but it followed the same pattern seen elsewhere — unverified claims used to justify disproportionate force, and public contracts flowing toward the politically connected.

Taken as a whole, the week showed two institutions moving in opposite directions. The judiciary, from district courts up through the circuit level, repeatedly blocked or narrowed administration efforts to purge voter rolls, restrict mail ballots, and compel state cooperation with federal subpoenas, maintaining what by week's end was a near-unbroken record of resistance on election-related questions. The Supreme Court, by contrast, used the same week to remove a 90-year safeguard on the president's power to fire independent agency leaders and to close off judicial review of major immigration decisions affecting hundreds of thousands of people. Congress, briefly asserting itself through the war-powers vote, folded within two days under direct presidential confrontation, and a housing bill with overwhelming bipartisan support was held hostage to force passage of a voting-restriction measure. Sentences of thirty to one hundred years for protesters, handed down under a newly invoked terrorism framework, sat alongside a reflecting pool controlled by fencing and National Guard troops — different in scale, but part of a single week in which claims of threat, whether to national security or to public property, were repeatedly used to justify the concentration and exercise of power with diminishing institutional resistance outside the courts. ```

Title: A Court That Giveth and Taketh, a Presidency That Cashes In
Content:
```markdown This was the week the Supreme Court closed out its term, and it did so with a docket that refused to move in one direction. Within the span of a few days, the justices preserved constitutional guarantees in one case and dismantled a decades-old check on presidential power in the next. Running alongside the rulings was a second story, pieced together through financial disclosures and investigative reporting, showing a president whose family's wealth had grown by billions of dollars through ventures his own administration regulates. By week's end, the two threads — judicial power and presidential profit — had become impossible to separate from the broader question of what checks remain on the executive.

**The Weekend**

The week opened on a somber note. On Saturday, the Supreme Court ruled 6-3 to let the administration strip Temporary Protected Status from roughly 350,000 Haitians and thousands of Syrians, clearing the way for deportations even to Haiti, a country under an active State Department travel warning. The ruling set the tone for an enforcement push that would intensify through the week. That same weekend, civic groups including 50501, the Women's March, and the Next250 coalition staged counter-programming to the administration's official 250th-anniversary events, asserting a fuller account of the nation's history. The administration's own "Freedom 250" fair on the National Mall, by contrast, drew sparse crowds despite heavy promotion, with Fox News hosts falsely describing it as packed and performers withdrawing once they recognized its partisan character. The White House also unveiled a commemorative passport bearing Trump's own portrait and signature, and Speaker Mike Johnson warned a conservative audience that a Democratic House majority would use its committees to investigate Trump's family and donors — an admission, of sorts, of what might be found. In Mississippi, police used teargas against demonstrators seeking accountability for the shooting death of a one-year-old child, while officials withheld the body-camera footage.

**Monday**

By Monday, the Court's term-ending docket began in earnest, and a separate story broke that would recur throughout the week: a Guardian investigation revealed that the White House's National Design Studio, staffed by veterans of the Department of Government Efficiency, had quietly rebuilt sensitive federal websites — a government login gateway, passport applications, children's savings accounts — operating outside the agencies legally responsible for them, without the privacy filings or spending disclosures normally required. The systems handled identity, financial, and passport data for millions of Americans, built and run by a parallel structure largely invisible to statutory oversight. It was, in its quiet way, one of the week's most significant stories: a structural expansion of executive reach that would outlast any single ruling.

The Court itself handed down two major and divergent decisions that day. In Slaughter v. Trump, a 6-3 majority overturned Humphrey's Executor, the 91-year-old precedent that had shielded heads of independent agencies from removal without cause. Adopting a "unitary executive" theory, the ruling gave the president sweeping new control over roughly two dozen agencies Congress had designed to operate independently of direct political control — a decision dissenting justices warned would reshape the structure of the federal government itself. Yet the same day, in a 5-4 ruling, the Court blocked Trump's attempted removal of Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, finding he had failed to provide the legally required notice and allowing her to remain on the board while her challenge proceeded. The Court, in other words, expanded removal power broadly while drawing a narrow, almost surgical line to protect the Fed's independence specifically. The justices also declined to hear Trump's final appeal of the $5 million E. Jean Carroll defamation verdict, closing out that chapter with the judgment intact.

Monday's immigration developments compounded the weekend's TPS ruling. North Carolina's legislature overrode gubernatorial vetoes to mandate sheriff cooperation with ICE and to pass anti-DEI education measures, while DHS Secretary Mullin defended deportations to Haiti despite the standing travel warning — a defense Ohio's Republican governor, Mike DeWine, publicly broke with. Elsewhere, reporting showed the administration had redirected funding from more than 900 National Park Service safety and maintenance projects while proposing to cut park staff by nearly a third, even as it sought $10 billion from Congress for Washington beautification, a request the Senate rejected. North Carolina's Senate advanced a bill criminalizing homeless encampments, even as Seattle and New York swore in new Democratic socialist mayors, Katie Wilson and Zohran Mamdani, the latter soon securing a rent freeze covering nearly a million apartments. At the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth continued an unexplained purge of senior military leadership, removing more than two dozen officers including the former Joint Chiefs chair and top Navy, Coast Guard, and Army leadership.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday brought the Court back to more protective ground. The justices rejected a Republican National Committee challenge to state laws counting mail-in ballots postmarked by Election Day, ruled that geofence warrants require Fourth Amendment protection, and agreed to hear a future case on proof-of-citizenship voting requirements. Away from the Court, Republican Senator Bill Cassidy publicly accused Trump of treating Congress "as an appendage" after being berated over his support for an Iran war-powers resolution — a rare public break from a sitting Republican senator over military transparency, though Cassidy later withdrew his support once belatedly briefed. Trump, meanwhile, dismissed a bipartisan housing bill that had passed 358-32 as "a big yawn," conditioning his signature on passage of the SAVE Act and blaming Republican holdouts including Lisa Murkowski. Legal resistance widened on multiple fronts: the Justice Department sued Massachusetts and Rhode Island over in-state tuition for undocumented students, federal employee unions sued over disability accommodations, 23 states challenged a Medicaid work-requirement rule, and courts granted injunctions protecting Seattle and Shoreline from DEI-related funding conditions. Trump also declared a fertilizer emergency to permit duty-free phosphate imports from Morocco and threatened to prosecute gas station owners who failed to lower prices — a threat Treasury Secretary Bessent would later echo.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday delivered the week's most consequential cluster of rulings. In Trump v. Barbara, the Court upheld birthright citizenship, striking down Trump's executive order and affirming the 14th Amendment's guarantee for children born on U.S. soil — a genuine preservation of a foundational constitutional right, though the margin was narrower than expected, with four justices expressing openness to revisiting the precedent in the future. In a separate 6-3 ruling, the Court upheld state bans on transgender athletes in women's sports, overturning lower-court decisions in Idaho and West Virginia and clearing the way for similar bans across roughly 25 other states. A third ruling eliminated limits on coordinated party campaign spending, extending a two-decade trend of dismantling campaign finance restrictions.

Away from the Court, HHS restructured its civil rights office to elevate religious exemptions, a move legal experts warned could enable healthcare providers to refuse care related to LGBTQ+ health, reproductive services, and vaccines. An HHS report found at least 5 million Americans had lost health insurance in the first half of the year due to the end of ACA subsidies — a loss Dr. Oz publicly minimized by suggesting exercise could offset healthcare costs. The Atlantic reported internal White House discussion of a "250 pardons for 250 years" initiative, alongside accounts of pardons being offered through international lobbying for roughly $2 million. And early reporting previewed Trump's forthcoming financial disclosure, pointing to $2.2 billion in earnings, much of it from cryptocurrency.

**Thursday**

By Thursday, the week's threads began to converge. One day after the Court upheld birthright citizenship, Acting Attorney General Blanche directed federal prosecutors to pursue fraud charges in "birth tourism" cases — despite acknowledging the practice accounts for less than one percent of U.S. births — an apparent attempt to narrow through enforcement what the Court had just affirmed. A federal judge separately blocked a USPS plan to deny mail-ballot delivery to states that refused to share voter rolls with DHS, the second judicial setback for the administration's mail-voting restrictions in recent weeks. Florida's state education board voted to bar undocumented and non-citizen students from all 28 public universities, a move critics said exceeded its authority. In New York, nearly half a million residents lost coverage as the state's Essential Plan ended, a direct consequence of federal Medicaid cuts and the expiration of ACA subsidies.

ICE arrested more than 10,000 people in five days, nearly doubling its prior daily pace, while new student loan borrowing caps and the elimination of income-driven repayment plans took effect. New reporting detailed Trump's substantial NVIDIA and Amazon holdings while he set policy affecting those firms, stock purchases made ahead of his own tariff-pause announcement, and an undisclosed $50 million loan. And in a case testing the boundaries of military dissent, an active-duty Air Force officer, Major Jason Watson, was arrested in uniform while holding a sign calling for Trump and Vance's impeachment; the Air Force opened an investigation that could end his career.

**Friday**

The week closed with its heaviest convergence yet. The Court weakened the Voting Rights Act, giving southern legislatures greater latitude to redraw districts previously protected to ensure minority representation — a decision experts said would meaningfully reduce the number of Black representatives in Congress. A House Democratic investigation titled "From Vanity to Insanity" alleged the 250th-anniversary celebration had been turned into a vehicle for self-dealing, with donor funds routed through a shadow entity, sponsorships sold for access, and civic programming replaced by partisan content.

Trump's 927-page ethics disclosure confirmed the $2.2 billion in earnings previewed earlier in the week, more than $1.4 billion of it from family crypto ventures, even as the SEC eased enforcement on exchanges listing his coin and the Senate Banking Committee voted down a measure barring presidential crypto ownership. Separate reporting showed Trump's sons had taken a 20 percent stake in a company tied to a Kazakhstan mining deal secured by the administration, and that at least 14 companies connected to the Trump and Lutnick families had received or were being considered for $8.9 billion in federal funding.

In New Orleans, a judge sealed his courtroom in violation of state law during the indictment of the state's attorney general, and journalists who objected were handcuffed — a decision the state supreme court later stayed over the procedural violations. The Fifth Circuit, meanwhile, ruled that the government cannot detain immigrants longer than 90 days without a bond hearing, restoring a measure of judicial review amid the enforcement surge. The administration allocated $68 million to a politically connected contractor for its July 4th celebration, while federally funded "Freedom Trucks" exhibits presented a sanitized version of American history omitting slavery and Native removal. And legal experts, echoing Speaker Johnson's warning from the weekend, predicted that a Democratic House majority would move quickly to investigate alleged corruption, a proposed slush fund, and possible emoluments violations.

Taken as a whole, the week offers a rare, condensed view of a government institution pulling in two directions at once. The Supreme Court affirmed birthright citizenship and mail-ballot access even as it stripped humanitarian protections from hundreds of thousands of people, gutted a long-standing check on presidential removal power, and narrowed voting-rights protections that had shaped congressional representation for half a century — often by margins thin enough to invite reversal. Set against that judicial record, the week's financial disclosures turned what had been reported allegation into documented fact: a sitting president earning billions from an industry his administration regulates, with family members profiting from government-brokered deals abroad and a shadow web infrastructure handling citizens' data beyond the reach of ordinary oversight. Courts, state officials, journalists, and even members of the president's own party pushed back at nearly every turn — through injunctions, public dissent, and investigative reporting — but the week's cumulative record suggests an executive branch testing, and in several cases finding, the limits of what existing checks can still restrain. ```

Title: A Semiquincentennial of Spectacle, Shootings, and Strained Alliances
Content:
```markdown The country's 250th anniversary fell this week, and the week that followed showed, in compressed form, nearly every strand of tension that has come to define American public life: ceremony bent toward politics, federal force turned lethal against bystanders, alliances tested abroad, and courts repeatedly asked to hold the line at home. It began with fireworks and a flag-draped stage, and it ended with a farmworker's death, a Senate campaign's collapse, and a housing bill signed into law without the president's signature.

**The Weekend**

The weekend's commemorations set the tone. A storm-delayed, late-night address on the National Mall saw the president describe political opponents as communists and repeat claims of election fraud, and a follow-up speech at Mt. Rushmore called for voter-ID legislation and warned, without evidence, of a century of lost elections if it failed to pass. At one point he appeared to reference serving a third term before catching himself. What might have been a unifying national commemoration instead became an occasion for campaign rhetoric and a preview of fights over voting rules that would recur throughout the week.

The celebration carried a literal toll as well. An 850,000-firework display — roughly 121 times the previous year's show — released an estimated nine metric tons of toxic compounds into the air over a major American city, triggering a Code Red and then a Code Purple air-quality alert, thousands of emergency calls, and hospital visits. Internal documents suggested officials had anticipated the pollution beforehand. Separately, hundreds of masked Patriot Front marchers carried Confederate flags through the capital chanting "Reclaim America," and the White House did not respond to questions about whether the president condemned the demonstration. Days later, a House Natural Resources Committee report alleged that congressional funds meant for the bipartisan America250 program had instead been routed to a parallel "Freedom 250" entity, including payments to the firm that organized the rally preceding the January 6th Capitol riot — adding a financial dimension to the weekend's political theater.

Other threads emerged early and would develop through the week. Reporting revealed that nearly a million people lost a combined $3.81 billion on the president's memecoin as its value collapsed 97 percent, while he personally extracted $636 million in upfront fees — a stark asymmetry between presidential profit and public loss that drew little formal response. On the Democratic side, early fractures surfaced in Senate primary contests: Dan Goldman lost his Brooklyn primary to a more pro-Palestinian challenger, Mallory McMorrow withdrew from Michigan's race, and a Brooklyn café's refusal to serve Goldman drew a federal civil rights inquiry. In Maine, allegations against Senate nominee Graham Platner began building pressure that would culminate later in the week. And in an unrelated but telling episode, the president personally called FIFA's president to reverse a red-card suspension against a U.S. soccer player — the first such reversal since 1962 — drawing international notice to the reach of his personal interventions.

**Tuesday**

By Tuesday, the week's gravest story began. An ICE officer in Houston shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a 52-year-old construction worker who had lived in the United States for 35 years, during what officials described as a mistaken-identity traffic stop. The Department of Homeland Security claimed Salgado Araujo had "weaponized" his vehicle; his family and three witnesses who had been riding with him disputed that account. No body-camera footage existed. The Harris County Medical Examiner would go on to rule the death a homicide. The case would not recede over the following days — it would deepen.

The same day, the Supreme Court narrowed legal protections for immigrants in two separate rulings. A 6-3 decision held that Temporary Protected Status determinations are largely shielded from judicial review, threatening status for more than a million people, including over 300,000 Haitians. A second ruling approved reinstatement of the "metering" policy limiting asylum claims at the southern border. Later reporting would detail the practical consequences: tens of thousands of healthcare and caregiving workers stood to lose work authorization, compounding an existing caregiver shortage. Against this, the 11th Circuit struck down the higher-education provision of Florida's Stop Woke Act in a 2-1 ruling, finding the state had been "puppeteering" educators' speech on race and gender — one of several moments this week in which courts pushed back against expansive state or federal authority even as other rulings narrowed protections elsewhere.

**Wednesday**

On Wednesday, attention shifted to a NATO summit that unraveled in public view. The president criticized allies for not backing strikes on Iran, ordered a trade cutoff with Spain over a base-access dispute, confused Iran with Japan and Zelensky with Putin, and used rhetoric toward Iran's civilian infrastructure that observers described as genocidal. A German official said plainly that "Europeans don't take Trump seriously any longer." Amid an alleged credible missile threat, the Secret Service moved the president through a catering truck to a smaller aircraft while journalists and senior officials remained aboard the original Air Force One as an apparent decoy, with reporters ordered to lower their window shades — leaving the people meant to document the presidency unknowingly serving as a shield for it.

The same day, back in Houston, three eyewitnesses to Salgado Araujo's shooting — including his brother — were detained by ICE at an undisclosed location, prompting fear among family and advocates that they would be deported before they could testify. The Justice Department simultaneously escalated pressure on state election administration, sending letters to all 50 states threatening criminal prosecution over noncitizen-voting claims, announcing election monitors for Democratic-leaning jurisdictions in six states, and demanding voter data from Lansing, Michigan. In a separate but related legal track, Judge Lewis Kaplan ordered release of the $5.8 million judgment E. Jean Carroll had won against the president, after the Supreme Court declined to review the case; the president immediately filed notice of appeal. Defense Secretary Hegseth also announced a new Pentagon-DOJ taskforce to prosecute unauthorized press disclosures, while a military officer who had called for impeachment was restricted to base under a gag order — a pairing of actions aimed, in different ways, at narrowing dissent.

**Thursday**

By Thursday, courts continued to reject delay. The Second Circuit denied the administration's bid to postpone the Carroll payment, and the D.C. Circuit rejected a request to pause the removal of the president's name from the Kennedy Center, finding no evidence to support the administration's claimed financial harm. In a separate and striking move, the president announced he would seek an unprecedented rehearing of the Supreme Court's recent decision upholding birthright citizenship — a ruling the Court had issued only a week earlier — calling it "wrong" and citing a Texas hospital's maternity marketing to Mexican mothers as evidence of "birth tourism." Meanwhile, in Houston, pressure for accountability sustained itself: DHS's own Inspector General, rather than an independent body, was assigned to investigate the shooting; Representative Sylvia Garcia demanded a full inquiry with evidence preservation; and hundreds marched down Canal Street building a memorial as LULAC offered a reward and gathered nearly 70,000 petition signatures. Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker, reacting to the NATO summit's confusion, publicly suggested the president was "suffering from dementia," injecting fitness-for-office questions into open political discourse.

**Friday**

Friday brought a second fatal immigration enforcement action, distinct from the one in Houston. Agents in tactical gear raided two California cannabis facilities operating as Glass House Farms, deploying chemical munitions against protesters. A 56-year-old farmworker, Jaime Alanis, fell 30 feet to his death during the operation. A U.S. Army veteran, George Retes, was detained for days without charge. In total, 375 people, including minors, were arrested. Both the Alanis family and Retes filed lawsuits. Coming less than a week after the Houston shooting, the raid marked a second instance of lethal federal immigration enforcement within the same cycle, reinforcing a pattern rather than an isolated episode.

The same day, the Graham Platner story reached its conclusion. Facing sexual assault allegations and resurfaced controversial social media posts, the Democratic Senate nominee in Maine withdrew his candidacy, ending a crisis that had drawn pressure from Bernie Sanders and most of the party's leadership — a resolution to a thread that had been building since the opening days of the week. Separately, the president declined to sign a bipartisan housing affordability bill that had passed with large majorities, stating he would withhold his signature "in protest" unless the Senate passed the SAVE America Act. The bill became law anyway at midnight without his signature, the constitutional process functioning despite the attempted leverage. The week closed with two further regulatory moves: a new rule cutting habitat protections for endangered species, described by environmentalists as the largest such rollback in fifty years, and a second War Powers Act notification on Iran that was interpreted internally as restarting the statute's 60-day clock — an interpretation legal analysts said had no basis in law. In Minnesota, Secretary of State Rubio revoked the legal status of a Laotian immigrant whom the governor had pardoned weeks earlier and had him deported, using the case to criticize state sanctuary policies.

Taken as a whole, the week showed a federal government reaching further into realms long governed by norms, process, and institutional restraint — commemorations turned partisan, alliances strained by confusion and threat, immigration enforcement resulting in two separate deaths within days of each other, and a demand to revisit a constitutional ruling barely a week old. But it also showed resistance built into the system rather than imposed from outside it: courts that refused delay tactics, an appeals panel that struck down a speech-restrictive law, a housing bill that became law despite an attempt to hold it hostage, and a grassroots mobilization in Houston that kept pressure on federal investigators who might otherwise have let a death go unexamined. The week did not resolve the tension between these forces. It simply made it visible, day by day, from a storm-delayed speech on the Mall to a farmworker's fall in a California field. ```
