Title: The Week Executive Power Stopped Asking Permission
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the presidency moved like an institution no longer waiting to be told no. Across seven days, the executive branch expanded military action without new congressional sign-off, converted a routine housing bill into leverage for voting restrictions, watched immigration agents kill three civilians who were not their targets, and closed with a nationally televised speech threatening the broadcast licenses of networks that declined to carry it. Courts, a scattering of Republicans, and journalists pushed back throughout, with results that were real but partial.

The pattern was visible before the weekend had properly started. Trump declined to sign a bipartisan housing bill, letting it become law automatically rather than attaching his name to it—a deliberate inaction meant to pressure the Senate into passing the Save America Act, a mail-in-ballot ban and voter-ID measure that lacked the votes to pass on its own. Around the same time, the administration notified Congress that hostilities with Iran had resumed, asserting a fresh 60-day war-powers clock despite having claimed only weeks earlier that a ceasefire was holding. Neither move asked permission. Both would recur, in variation, all week.

At Camp David, Trump convened a closed session on a reconciliation-based military funding package, inviting only hardline Freedom Caucus members and confiscating attendees' phones. Moderate Republicans were shut out entirely; one invitee who did attend indicated afterward that she would vote against the resulting package anyway. It was a small episode next to the week's larger stories, but it set a tone: negotiation narrowed to those already in agreement, dissent filtered out before it could reach the table.

Then came Houston. An ICE agent shot and killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, a business owner and father who was not the agency's intended target, amid a surge of enforcement activity staffed partly by agents hired without standard vetting. It was the first of three such deaths within the week, each in a different city, each involving someone the government had not set out to arrest. Almost simultaneously, the Justice Department subpoenaed four New York Times reporters to testify before a grand jury over their coverage of Secret Service concerns about the Qatari-donated Air Force One—a subpoena that followed an eight-hour FBI investigation directed from inside the White House. Press freedom and immigration enforcement, two of the week's defining threads, were both already in motion before Monday arrived.

Monday delivered the week's clearest instance of judicial pushback holding. Federal Judge Kathleen Williams voided a $10 billion lawsuit Trump had filed against the IRS, finding it had been filed in bad faith to manufacture a fraudulent $1.776 billion settlement that would have shielded Trump, his family, and his associates from tax-crime prosecution. She sanctioned his attorneys and referred some for professional discipline. It was a rare case of a court not merely slowing an executive maneuver but naming it for what it was and unwinding it outright.

The same day brought a second fatal ICE shooting, this one in Maine. Officer David Brouillette, hired despite a documented history of domestic-violence allegations and without standard vetting, killed Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a Colombian national authorized to work in the United States, during a vehicle stop with no body camera present. Separately, Trump removed three members of an independent federal commission that works with states on election administration, a move Senate Democrats characterized as interference ahead of the midterms. By proclamation, the administration also shrank the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante national monuments by roughly 90 percent each, stripping protection from nearly three million acres, disbanding the Bears Ears Commission, and opening the land to mining. And Trump tied renewal of an expired surveillance law to passage of the Save America Act—another unrelated priority pressed into service of the voting-restriction push.

Tuesday brought a third death connected to immigration enforcement: a 28-year-old man fleeing an ICE encounter at a Florida gas station was struck and killed by a tractor-trailer, on the very day border czar Tom Homan announced ICE would pause most vehicle stops to review procedures following the two prior shootings. The timing underscored how far operational pressure had outrun any attempt at reform. The same day, Mahmoud Khalil, detained for 104 days, sued Trump officials and allied groups under the Ku Klux Klan Act of 1871, alleging a coordinated campaign—branded internally as Project Esther—to identify and deport pro-Palestinian activists. A report from Physicians for Human Rights and UC Berkeley documented 203 injuries, including blindings and traumatic brain injuries, from 412 incidents of crowd-control weapon misuse against immigration-enforcement protesters over the preceding year, with federal officials responsible for nearly two-thirds of them; ICE separately pepper-sprayed Senator Andy Kim during a protest outside a New Jersey detention facility. And Trump removed Cathy Harris from the Merit Systems Protection Board, the body charged with protecting merit-based civil-service hiring, following reporting that the administration had secretly influenced an earlier MSPB ruling in its own favor.

By Wednesday, the one-day-old ICE vehicle-stop pause was gone. Trump personally insisted the stops continue as a "Crime Fighting tool," and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin fell in line, even as the department separately offered undocumented immigrants $2,600 to leave voluntarily. The reversal came less than 24 hours after the policy had been announced, and days after it had followed two fatal shootings of non-targets. Elsewhere, Senate Democrats under Chuck Schumer denied the $1.15 trillion defense authorization bill the votes needed to advance, citing ongoing military exchanges with Iran despite a war-powers resolution passed the previous month—a concrete assertion of congressional leverage against unauthorized warmaking. Trump imposed 25 percent tariffs on Brazil, timed to coincide with an election pitting Lula against Jair Bolsonaro's son, despite a documented U.S. trade surplus with Brazil that undercut the administration's stated rationale. And Todd Blanche, Trump's former personal attorney and acting attorney general, began a contentious confirmation hearing in which he was pressed on both his role in the voided IRS settlement and his handling of redacted Epstein files.

Thursday was the week's loudest day. In a primetime address, Trump revived claims that China had accessed 2020 voter data and that the CIA had covered it up, directed federal agencies to investigate and potentially prosecute officials over the alleged coverup, and called for revoking the broadcast licenses of NBC and ABC after they declined to air the speech live—an escalation FCC Chair Brendan Carr had already signaled he might support. Within hours, the claims collapsed under their own weight. CNN and Senator Mark Warner publicly debunked the specifics; Representative Thomas Massie contradicted the voter-data framing; and John Solomon, the White House's own hired analyst behind the underlying report, admitted on camera that "the intel community has zero evidence" of vote-flipping in 2020, 2022, or 2024. The speech's central claim was dismantled not by adversaries but by the man commissioned to support it.

The same day, the House passed the Save America Act 217–209 along party lines, attaching it to a State Department spending bill destined for a Senate filibuster—the culmination of a week spent tying the measure to unrelated legislation. A House vote to cut $3.3 billion in Israel military aid failed 314–104, but more than 100 Democrats, including Nancy Pelosi and Whip Katherine Clark, broke with leadership to support it, exposing a generational split inside the party. And FBI Director Kash Patel and Chief of Staff Susie Wiles personally ran a White House-directed leak investigation into the Air Force One reporting, confiscating officials' phones, while Stephen Miller delivered a speech describing political opponents in dehumanizing terms and launching a rhetorical campaign against what he called "radical left terrorism."

Friday closed the loop on several of the week's threads. DHS Secretary Mullin warned state election officials they would be treated as investigative priorities if they refused to run voter rolls through a federal matching tool that courts have blocked sixteen times, while Trump separately ordered DHS to direct states to deem noncitizens ineligible to vote using that same disputed tool. The FBI notified staff it would no longer independently investigate violent encounters involving ICE agents—removing, by week's end, the oversight mechanism that had previously produced evidence used to prosecute agents in such cases. A panel of federal judges unanimously appointed Roger Rogoff as U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington; Trump fired him about an hour after he took the oath. And despite testimony from a former DOJ pardon attorney alleging retaliatory firing, and judicial criticism over the voided IRS settlement, the Senate confirmed Todd Blanche as attorney general.

The week did not end only in executive consolidation. Over 600 communities began a weekend of voter registration drives, teach-ins, and vigils honoring the late Representative John Lewis, alongside a bipartisan petition against a border-wall project and continued protests near ICE facilities—among them a shooting of a protester by an off-duty detention-center employee. The civic response ran on its own track, parallel to the week's official actions rather than growing out of them.

Taken together, the week showed an executive branch testing boundaries on several fronts simultaneously rather than one at a time: war powers, voting rules, press oversight, civil-service protections, and lethal force in immigration enforcement all moved in the same seven days, each reinforcing the others. Institutional resistance was neither absent nor sufficient—a federal judge voided a fraudulent settlement and sanctioned the lawyers who built it, a Senate majority leader denied a defense bill its votes, a hired analyst contradicted his own commissioned report, and hundreds of communities organized in the streets. But a safety pause ordered after two deaths lasted barely a day, an oversight body lost its members, an independently appointed prosecutor lost his job within the hour, and a Cabinet confirmation proceeded despite documented concerns about its nominee's fitness. The ledger from this week will not be settled by any single verdict; it will be read, instead, in which of these countervailing forces proves durable once the next week begins. ```
Excerpt: This week showed an executive branch testing how far it could extend without resistance from Congress or the courts.

Title: War Funding, Vanishing Casualties, and a Voting Bill Riding Shotgun on Defense Policy
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which the gap between what Washington said and what Washington did became the story itself. The Iran war entered its fifth month with the Pentagon asking for tens of billions more in funding even as it grew less transparent about the war's human cost, while House Republicans used a defense bill to carry voting restrictions that could not pass on their own, and states lined up in federal court to challenge a push to tie disaster aid to election rules. By week's end, Congress had voted twice to assert control over a war it could not actually stop, and the administration had extended its reach from the battlefield into the halls of the Smithsonian.

The weekend set the tone. President Trump directed the Department of Homeland Security to flag noncitizens on state voter rolls and pressed Congress to pass the Save America Act, while Secretary Markwayne Mullin threatened state officials with prosecution for declining to use a verification tool that courts had already blocked. Stephen Bannon floated invoking a national-security emergency order to force the law through. At the same time, Secretary of State Rubio warned of "Radical Left terrorism" even as data continued to show right-wing political violence far more prevalent — rhetoric delivered against a backdrop of hundreds of coordinated protests over ICE shootings, voter suppression, and AI datacenter expansion. Also emerging over the weekend was the first indication of a story that would recur all week: in the days before an Iranian strike killed two U.S. soldiers, the Pentagon had not disclosed three earlier attacks on American forces in Jordan that injured dozens of troops. A federal immigration agent with a documented history of domestic violence allegedly shot and killed a Colombian immigrant in Maine, and reporting indicated the FBI had quietly stopped investigating ICE confrontations despite a string of killings, even as DOJ and DHS denied it. Amid this, the Third Circuit became the first federal appeals court to strike down a state assault weapons ban, setting up likely Supreme Court review of similar laws in more than ten states, and the bipartisan 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act became law over Trump's objection — a rare legislative achievement as the House Judiciary chair acknowledged Congress was essentially finished legislating before the midterms.

By Monday, the administration's attention turned outward and backward at once. Trump signed three proclamations imposing 50 percent tariffs on Canadian automobiles, dairy, and alcohol, citing discriminatory trade practices and wildfire smoke; Canadian officials called it a violation of the USMCA and warned of damage to a decades-long alliance. The Justice Department sought broad phone records belonging to New York Times reporters and their relatives in connection with reporting on a Qatar-donated Air Force One, before withdrawing the subpoenas amid accusations of intimidation. A ceremonial Captive Nations Week proclamation framed communism as the gravest foreign threat in language that blurred the line between authoritarian regimes abroad and political dissent at home. Meanwhile, gasoline hit $4 a gallon nationally and Brent crude surged past $91 as the widening Iran conflict rattled energy markets. The ACLU sued HHS over a childcare funding freeze based on unverified claims from a viral video, the Justice Department found UC San Diego's medical school had violated civil rights law through its admissions practices, and reporting revealed that corporate PACs — SpaceX, Home Depot, Walmart, Toyota, and Google among them — had funneled hundreds of thousands of dollars to lawmakers sponsoring bills expanding ICE's authority. In a smaller but telling counter-development, ICE announced it would require body cameras for vehicle stops following the fatal shootings, and Citizens Bank ended its financing relationships with private prison operators running ICE facilities.

Tuesday brought the week's first direct reckoning over the war's true scope. Defense Secretary Hegseth appeared before the Senate requesting a $454 billion defense budget increase along with $67 billion in emergency Iran war funding, and senators from both parties pressed him on contradictions — about Iran's remaining military capability, about unauthorized strikes in the Caribbean, and about whether the war had any congressional authorization at all. The same day, Trump declared that Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu would not be arrested in the United States under any circumstances, overriding an outstanding International Criminal Court warrant and asserting personal authority over a matter normally left to domestic law enforcement. Courts, meanwhile, delivered a mixed set of rulings: a fired U.S. Attorney sued over his removal less than an hour after being appointed, a federal appeals court upheld Peter Navarro's contempt convictions, and a Washington suburb ended a license-plate surveillance contract after documented abuse — even as reporting showed ICE had failed to equip most officers with body cameras despite having the funding to do so. HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. announced withholding more than $1 billion in additional Medicaid funds from California and Minnesota based on unsubstantiated fraud claims, layered atop funds already withheld since the previous year. Trump's own rhetoric sharpened further: he posted that Iran would "pay many times over" for the dead soldiers, falsely blamed immigrants for a fire actually set by a U.S. Army veteran, and mischaracterized Venezuela's crisis as a natural disaster.

Wednesday was when the voting-restrictions storyline fused formally with war funding. The House passed a $95 billion budget resolution allocating $73 billion for Iran war operations, $12 billion in farm aid, and $10 billion toward advancing the Save America Act — using the reconciliation process specifically to bypass the Senate filibuster. The same day, Brent crude climbed above $94 a barrel, Arizona terminated SNAP benefits for 440,000 residents under cuts in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, and the TSA began privatizing airport security screening at two airports, unwinding a post-9/11 federal safeguard. House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan referred former special counsel Jack Smith to the acting attorney general over alleged false testimony, a move Smith's lawyers called retaliation for his investigation of the president. Separate reporting found the United States had collected more than $13 billion from Venezuelan oil sales with no public accounting, an external review of the Gates Foundation documented roughly thirty undisclosed meetings between Bill Gates and Jeffrey Epstein between 2011 and 2014, and a federal judge ordered Trump to disclose financial details in his defamation suit against the BBC. In Madison, Wisconsin, a police officer fatally shot a man during an arrest, an incident captured on video that triggered local protests and a state-led independent investigation.

Thursday was arguably the week's hinge point for war oversight. The House passed a $1.15 trillion defense authorization bill that incorporated the Save America Act's mail-ballot ban and voter ID mandates alongside expanded U.S.-Israel defense cooperation — embedding a contested election policy inside legislation that is, in ordinary years, considered must-pass. On the same day, it emerged that the Pentagon had quietly reduced its official Iran war death toll from eighteen to fourteen, removing four service members killed after a declared ceasefire, a revision critics said appeared designed to avoid triggering war powers requirements tied to casualty thresholds. Trump told reporters he was close to deciding on a "massive attack" on Iran larger than any prior operation, and separately threatened to bomb Iranian bridges or power plants — a threat against civilian infrastructure that would, if carried out, violate international law. The administration also imposed new 10 to 12.5 percent tariffs on goods from more than eighty countries, citing forced-labor enforcement failures and invoking a different statutory authority than the one the Supreme Court had struck down months earlier; two small businesses immediately sued, even as the U.S. trade representative told the Senate tariffs were not raising prices, contradicting both inflation data and senators' own cost estimates. Brent crude crossed $100 a barrel that day, up 42 percent in twenty days, following Houthi attacks on Saudi tankers and Iranian strikes near the Iraq-Kuwait border. Separate reporting detailed that officials overseeing $58.5 billion in Pentagon AI spending and a $20 billion private-equity-styled investment office held undisclosed personal financial stakes in related ventures, one tied to a Trump family member, while Jim Jordan's referral of Jack Smith was formalized and former Barclays CEO Jes Staley testified before Congress about his past relationship with Jeffrey Epstein.

Friday brought the week's attempt at congressional reassertion — and its limits. The House passed, for the second time, a resolution directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran, joined by four Republicans, but the Senate narrowly rejected a nearly identical measure by a 47-49 vote. A senior Democrat moved to force litigation compelling compliance with existing war powers obligations the administration had simply ignored. The same day, a coalition of twenty-five states and the District of Columbia sued over FEMA and DHS conditions requiring paper ballots, citizenship verification, and immigration enforcement cooperation as prerequisites for more than $1 billion and $740 million in federal disaster and security grants. Trump signed an executive order directing federal agencies to post signage outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History warning visitors of alleged "ideological capture" and pointing them to alternative historical sources — a formal federal directive, backed by physical signage, extending a rhetorical campaign against the museum's curatorial independence into government action. Courts again delivered a mixed record: judges blocked the termination of work authorization for asylum seekers and TPS holders, ruled FDA restrictions on mifepristone arbitrary and ordered reconsideration, and the Fourth Circuit rejected an attempt to redetain a Georgetown scholar over pro-Palestinian speech, while a dozen states won a temporary block on the Paramount-Warner Bros merger. But a federal panel declined to block a Tennessee redistricting map that splits Memphis's Black population across three districts. The Justice Department sued Milwaukee over its ban on masked, unidentified federal agents and sued Colorado over in-state tuition for undocumented students — its fourteenth such suit nationally — while Trump ordered ICE to resume vehicle stops despite a safety suspension put in place after a fatal shooting, even as a congressional briefing revealed only one disciplinary referral among fifty-six excessive-force complaints against ICE officers. The week closed with reporting that federal debt held by the public had exceeded 100 percent of GDP, even as the administration requested an additional $11.1 billion in agricultural assistance, pushing total 2026 farm support above $55 billion.

Taken as a whole, the week illustrated how difficult it has become to separate the machinery of war from the machinery of domestic politics. A defense budget swelled while the public accounting of the war it funded grew less reliable, not more. Congress exercised its constitutional war powers twice and was overruled or ignored both times, while a policy that could not survive ordinary legislative debate was carried instead inside a bill few in Congress would vote against. States went to court by the dozens to defend their authority over elections and disaster relief, courts split between checking and permitting executive action, and an order aimed at how history itself is presented in a national museum showed that the week's exercises of power were not confined to the battlefield or the ballot box. Nothing was resolved by Friday; much of it had simply been pushed, unresolved, into the weeks ahead. ```
Excerpt: This week was dominated by the widening gap between what the administration said about the Iran war and what the record showed.

Title: This Week in Democracy: History Rewritten, Powers Tested, and a Nomination Held Hostage
Content:
```markdown # This Week in Democracy: History Rewritten, Powers Tested, and a Nomination Held Hostage

*Week 80 – July 25–31, 2026*

The week of July 25–31 moved on three parallel tracks that, by its end, had become difficult to separate: a sustained effort to control how federal institutions present American history, a military and economic standoff with Iran that generated both inflated rhetoric and real casualties, and a Justice Department confirmation fight that turned on the president's personal finances. Courts and a handful of senators pushed back at several points, but the overall trajectory was one of executive authority testing its limits while the usual checks strained to keep up.

**The Weekend**

The weekend set the tone. A Trump-appointed preservation board voted to gut Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, eliminating six decades of required public and tribal consultation before federal agencies alter historic sites. The timing was not incidental: a disputed triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and a proposal to open the Chaco Canyon buffer zone, a UNESCO World Heritage Indigenous site, to mineral extraction were both already drawing legal objections. The same weekend, an executive order directed officials to post signs outside the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History declaring its exhibits inaccurate, building on a White House report accusing the museum of bias. It was the opening move in what would become a week-long campaign against the institution.

Economic and military policy moved in tandem. After the Supreme Court struck down the administration's emergency tariffs, the president tried Section 122 of the Trade Act, then pivoted to Section 301 as a 150-day deadline lapsed, citing forced-labor justifications. Legal analysts noted the maneuvering could let tariffs persist indefinitely without congressional approval — a workaround, not a retreat. Second-quarter GDP growth came in at 1.5%, well below forecasts, with economists tying the shortfall to Iran war disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz and tariff-driven price increases. Meanwhile, four House Republicans joined Democrats in a symbolic vote demanding troop withdrawal from Iran — a small but real crack in party unity — even as border czar Tom Homan acknowledged on television that an ICE officer involved in a fatal shooting should never have cleared vetting given a documented history of abuse.

**Monday**

The ICE vetting concern had become a pattern rather than an isolated admission. After fatal shootings in Texas and Maine prompted a brief pause in vehicle stops, the president ordered enforcement resumed despite the documented risk, and the family of one victim, Longoria, filed a federal lawsuit alleging a violation of both use-of-force policy and a standing court order against racial profiling.

The same day produced a different kind of harm. The New York Post published an unverified claim that thousands of 9/11 families wanted Mayor Mamdani excluded from an anniversary ceremony. Within hours, Fox Business, Fox News, and CBS New York had echoed or amplified it, and the claimed signature count inflated from roughly 1,100 to as high as 15,000 as it spread. Separately, Taylor Farms lobbied the White House to delay public disclosure of a multi-state cyclospora outbreak linked to its products, a request a former FDA commissioner said fell outside normal practice.

At a Michigan rally that evening, the president added to a growing list of unsubstantiated claims — asserting he had attended a G20 summit he had in fact boycotted, making false statements about ammunition stockpiles, posting AI-generated images including a fabricated movie poster, and declining to say where $13 billion in seized Venezuelan assets had gone. Senate Majority Leader John Thune acknowledged that the votes did not exist to repeal the filibuster for the president's SAVE America Act, with at least fifteen Republican senators opposed under any circumstance. And in the Arizona borderlands, federal contractors felled ancient cottonwood trees for wall construction despite an earlier no-fell pledge, touching off a tree-sit occupation, while the administration asked the Supreme Court to fully enforce its blocked mail-voting executive order.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday was the week's most crowded day. The president pressed Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to deepen cuts to the childhood immunization schedule despite a federal judge having already blocked such changes and internal polling showing the move unpopular — a direct push against judicial restraint during a period of rising measles cases. In New Jersey, a routine software error that had allowed fewer than 400 noncitizens to vote, already corrected with no fraud or changed outcomes found, became the basis for House Republican hearings, a federal probe, and a Homeland Security official's claim that a single illegal vote "cancels out" a citizen's.

The FCC opened a license-renewal challenge against eight ABC-owned stations over editorial content, a move a bipartisan group of former FCC officials warned violated both the Communications Act and the Constitution. Senator Mitch McConnell, six weeks after a hospitalizing fall and still uncleared to resume duties, faced a formal demand from Kentucky's governor that he prove his fitness or resign, with an August 3 deadline for calling a special election looming.

Rhetoric around Iran escalated sharply: in a Fox interview, the president claimed personal control over the Strait of Hormuz, asserted he had halted eight wars including an India-Pakistan nuclear standoff, and threatened to destroy Iranian bridges and power plants within hours absent a deal, as Iran's Revolutionary Guard threatened to close the strait and Saudi refineries reportedly burned. The day closed on a different note at Senator Lindsey Graham's funeral, where a Fox host's eulogy focused on praising the president rather than the deceased, and senior aide Stephen Miller described Democratic leaders as "freaks, weirdos, losers, and crazies" on air.

Quietly, the 9/11 story began to unravel: Popular Information reported that the petition's organizer had no verified list of victims' families, prompting CBS to revise its headline and the Post to silently alter its framing — neither issuing a transparent correction.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday brought the Smithsonian fight into open congressional view. A House subcommittee questioned museum director Anthea Hartig over alleged bias, and a committee member was found to have coordinated hearing questions with Christian nationalist activists who, despite lacking historical credentials, had been shaping White House museum policy directly. Vice President Vance delayed Board of Regents nominations to allow more ideologically aligned appointments, while the administration threatened to withhold federal funding from the institution altogether — three simultaneous levers of pressure on one museum system.

CBS, meanwhile, removed its social media posts about the Mamdani petition after privately acknowledging inaccuracies, but left the original article uncorrected online, citing a division between its national and local news operations. In Madison, police forcibly cleared a community memorial for Corey Ruiz, a man killed by officers, resulting in sixteen arrests and further confrontations that night.

**Thursday**

Thursday carried multiple major threads at once. At a Senate hearing on Covid origins, Dr. Anthony Fauci invoked his Fifth Amendment right rather than answer questions from Senator Rand Paul, who has previously called for his imprisonment; Paul announced he would pursue a contempt of Congress vote the following week.

The attorney general confirmation of Todd Blanche stalled when Senators Cornyn and Tillis demanded written assurance that a $1.8 billion fund tied to the president's personal IRS settlement would be eliminated. The president first called the fund "dead," then reversed course, vowing to revive it and threatening to withdraw Blanche's nomination simply to wait out the two senators' terms while keeping him as acting attorney general indefinitely. In the same stretch, the Senate unanimously opposed any pardon for Ghislaine Maxwell, Epstein survivors delivered documentary files to Senate offices, and the Justice Department complied with a judge's order to produce unredacted Epstein files for private review — a sign that judicial pressure could still extract partial transparency even amid the standoff.

The Pentagon, separately, revised Iran war casualty figures upward to 18 dead and 624 wounded after public scrutiny restored previously removed names. The president invoked Defense Production Act authority over critical minerals, delegating export-restriction power to the Commerce Secretary, and announced a $22 million purchase of 250 Cadillac Escalades for the White House fleet even as Americans faced rising gas prices and war-related costs exceeding $1,200 per household. A mislabeled, AI-generated map of Africa displayed at a State Department-linked health conference in Brazil added an embarrassing coda.

Asked about the 9/11 petition story, the president endorsed its premise directly, telling a reporter that victims' families were "very unhappy" with Mayor Mamdani — reviving a claim CBS's own reporting had already undercut. And a court-appointed monitor found California's largest ICE facility out of compliance with all eight court-ordered healthcare standards, as San Jose residents rallied against a proposed detention facility by invoking the history of Japanese American internment.

**Friday**

The week closed with two failures of legislative restraint and one of personal concession. The Senate voted 49–50 against a resolution requiring troop withdrawal from Iran absent explicit authorization, with only three Republicans in support — the second such attempt to fail within two weeks. The president declined Republican senators' request to formally limit his tax-immunity fund, deepening the Blanche standoff and demanding the Senate cancel its August recess to pass his legislative priority instead.

Immigration enforcement widened further: the administration ended federal legal-representation funding for more than 20,000 unaccompanied immigrant children, briefly offered a no-bid $150 million contract to a Trump-connected law firm before withdrawing it under public pressure, and confirmed that a detained hunger striker had been subjected to forced medical treatment. Pima County reported nineteen migrant deaths in July, the highest monthly total since 2024.

Courts offered a counterweight on voting rights: the Kansas Court of Appeals blocked an attempt to discard mail ballots arriving after Election Day, preserving a grace period protecting tens of thousands of votes, even as the administration pressed the Supreme Court to enforce its mail-voting order and the FBI was reported to have obtained a voter's IP address in a fraud inquiry a former Justice Department official called a "fishing expedition." California announced its minimum wage would rise to $17.40 an hour in 2027, a state-level response to what the governor described as federal inaction on wages.

Taken together, the week showed executive power advancing along several fronts at once — over historical memory, trade policy, immigration enforcement, war powers, and now the appointment of the nation's chief law enforcement officer — while the institutions meant to check that power produced mixed results. Courts blocked some actions and compelled partial disclosure in others. A bipartisan handful of senators held firm against eliminating the filibuster and against confirming an attorney general without conditions. But two war powers votes failed, a disinformation campaign reached millions before any real correction, and children lost legal representation as enforcement expanded. The record of the week suggests not a single dramatic rupture but a steady accumulation of tests — of historical truth, of institutional independence, of due process — whose cumulative weight will be easier to assess with distance than it was to see in real time. ```

Title: This Week in Democracy: Birthright Citizenship Defied, a Fund Dies to Confirm an Attorney General, and ICE's Record Month
Content:
```markdown The first week of August unfolded as a study in the uses and limits of presidential power: a week in which the executive repeatedly tested boundaries set by courts, Congress, and the Constitution, sometimes retreating under pressure and sometimes pressing forward in open defiance. By week's end, record immigration enforcement figures, a contested attorney general confirmation, and a presidential answer to a Supreme Court defeat had converged into a single narrative about how far executive authority could be stretched before something gave way.

**The Weekend**

The administration escalated a fight with the Smithsonian, issuing an executive order that accused the National Museum of American History of "extreme political activism" and mandated warning signage—part of a broader campaign reportedly shaped by activist David Barton's influence over how the administration wanted national history told. At the same time, a brewing standoff over the attorney general nomination surfaced publicly: with Senators John Cornyn and Thom Tillis blocking Todd Blanche's confirmation over a disputed $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund, Trump threatened to simply keep Blanche on as acting attorney general indefinitely, sidestepping the Senate's confirmation role altogether. Elsewhere, Trump Media's new "Truth API" service began selling early access to the president's market-moving posts for up to $100,000 a month, drawing requests from senators for an SEC investigation into whether the arrangement converted presidential communication into a vehicle for personal profit. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., amid a 35-year high in measles cases, urged parents to vaccinate their children while simultaneously calling vaccination a "personal choice" and repeating false claims linking vaccines to autism—a split message that did little to steady public confidence during an active outbreak. A mass shooting in Twin Falls, Idaho, that killed three people added a somber note to the weekend, while Texas's decision to pause new data center construction, following New York's earlier move, hinted at a shifting national posture toward AI infrastructure investment.

**Monday**

The week's legal and institutional fault lines began to widen. A coalition of 25 states, joined separately by 23 more states and the governors of Kentucky and Pennsylvania, filed suit in the Court of International Trade challenging tariffs that now covered 99.4 percent of all U.S. imports, arguing the duties exceeded statutory authority and defied an earlier Supreme Court tariff ruling. The same day, court records revealed that DHS and ICE had sought and obtained orders to force-feed at least ten detained immigrants since 2025, including an Afghan man restrained for nearly six months, frequently without legal representation present during the proceedings—a practice widely classified internationally as a form of torture. The Justice Department, meanwhile, announced a record 25 new denaturalization complaints, bringing the total since January 2025 to 123, part of what officials called the largest coordinated denaturalization effort in the department's history. In North Carolina, the state Senate passed a voter suppression bill without debating Democratic amendments; one senator invoked post-Reconstruction history before walking out, and protesters chanting in the gallery were removed from the chamber. James Comey's defense team filed motions alleging vindictive and selective prosecution, citing irregularities in the grand jury process, even as judges in multiple courts were separately reported describing Justice Department attorneys' conduct as "unlawful," "unethical," and "dishonest"—criticism tied partly to the collapsing Reflecting Pool vandalism case. That collapse fed directly into a presidential outburst: Trump spread false claims about the alleged vandalism on Truth Social, then attacked U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro by name for dropping the related charges, accusing her of having "folded like an umbrella."

**Tuesday**

The day brought a mixed set of judicial outcomes. In Arizona, federal contractors building border wall segments used broad statutory waivers to bypass the Endangered Species Act, felling cottonwood trees that housed nesting threatened birds—an example of executive authority overriding environmental law without legislative or judicial review. In a sharply different direction, a federal judge dismissed seditious conspiracy charges against Oath Keepers members tied to January 6, at the Justice Department's own request; the judge expressed regret that the case would not reach a different conclusion, a notable acknowledgment from the bench. Reporting also surfaced that ICE had detained a Johns Hopkins researcher and a University of Maryland pharmacy instructor, both holding valid work authorization, at U.S. airports, exposing inconsistencies in supposed enforcement priorities before both were released. Separately, new reporting found that billions of dollars in tariff refunds were flowing primarily to corporations rather than to the consumers who had actually borne the higher costs. Investigators also released surveillance and bodycam footage from the Twin Falls shooting, confirming the gunman had acted alone and that bystander intervention likely limited the casualty count.

**Wednesday**

The day offered a notable counterpoint to the week's pattern of executive assertion. In Missouri, voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required constitutional amendments to win majorities in every congressional district—a change that would have made future citizen-led amendments nearly impossible. In Kansas, voters rejected, for a second time, a proposal to replace judicial nominating commissions with direct elections for state Supreme Court justices. Both results preserved mechanisms that have protected reproductive rights, Medicaid expansion, and judicial independence from partisan restructuring. The same day, the White House revived its effort to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook, sending her a letter demanding a response to previously dismissed fraud allegations within three weeks, despite a Supreme Court ruling in June that had already allowed her to remain in her position. New Mexico's attorney general filed suit against the Justice Department, alleging it had reneged on a 2019 agreement to share unredacted investigative materials tied to Jeffrey Epstein's Zorro Ranch activities, obstructing the state's efforts to identify victims and co-conspirators. Trump's own legal team, meanwhile, moved to block a court order requiring him to disclose detailed financial records in his $10 billion defamation suit against the BBC, calling the demands "shockingly broad." And following a Supreme Court decision backing the administration, a judge lifted the stay protecting Temporary Protected Status for roughly 350,000 Haitian nationals; ICE began summoning Haitians in Ohio for ankle-monitor enforcement restricting their movement to within 75 miles of home.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the week's fulcrum. Weeks after the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 in Trump v. Barbara that Trump's original birthright citizenship order was unconstitutional, the president signed two new executive orders attempting to achieve similar ends through narrower categories, including a "birth tourism" framework, and called the Court's earlier decision "very unfortunate." The move amounted to a direct test of how far an administration could go in reformulating a policy after a definitive constitutional ruling against it. The same day, the Republican-led Senate Homeland Security Committee voted along party lines to hold Dr. Anthony Fauci in contempt of Congress after he invoked Fifth Amendment protections more than one hundred times during testimony; the committee had also controversially obtained a backup copy of his personal phone. Trump separately signed a proclamation imposing a 15 percent tariff and minimum import prices on polysilicon, a critical material for semiconductors and solar panels, citing national security and the collapse of domestic production capacity. ICE and TSA expanded airport enforcement operations, aiming for 2,000 daily immigration arrests and targeting people with pending visa and asylum applications, prompting some airlines to refuse cooperation absent judicial warrants. Journalist Georgia Fort, indicted for documenting a protest at a Minnesota church where an ICE official served as pastor, moved to dismiss her case, with her attorneys citing false statements in the search warrant applications and arguing the prosecution amounted to retaliation for her reporting. Trump also threatened "long term jail sentences" for officials who leaked information about U.S. munitions shortages tied to the Iran conflict, even as he denied the shortages existed. And the Justice Department's own internal watchdog, its Office of Professional Responsibility, was revealed to have received a record 1,666 misconduct complaints in 2025 even as its staff shrank from 29 to 16 and its director was fired without replacement.

**Friday**

Friday closed the week with resolution on several fronts. Todd Blanche's path to confirmation as attorney general finally cleared after Senator Bill Cassidy withdrew his opposition; the final holdout had been resolved only after Blanche agreed to terminate the disputed $1.8 billion anti-weaponization fund that had stalled his nomination for weeks, converting Monday's threat of unilateral acting authority into a negotiated, if contested, confirmation. The Washington Post reported that ICE arrests had hit a record monthly high of 43,000 in July, the largest total of Trump's second term, bringing detentions to more than 238,000 people over the year's first seven months, a pace apparently unaffected by recent controversies over fatal shootings involving agents. An Associated Press investigation separately found that at least 52 parents and spouses of active-duty service members had been detained since January 2025, with at least six deported, after a 2025 policy eliminated the longstanding bipartisan exemption protecting military families from deportation. ICE also announced a body-camera policy requiring every field officer to wear one by September, but the policy grants the agency's director discretion to delay or withhold footage of officer-involved deaths if release is not deemed "in the best interests of the agency," a provision drawing scrutiny following two recent fatal shootings that had gone unrecorded. An appeals court, meanwhile, reaffirmed that the White House ballroom project required congressional approval, finding no precedent for a president unilaterally demolishing taxpayer-funded portions of the White House—even as construction continued on the ground with a 250-person crew working around the clock. A Reuters analysis found that federal judges, including ten Republican appointees, had ruled against the administration in 75 of 93 cases raising First Amendment claims, spanning law firm retaliation, journalist restrictions, university funding cuts, and protest-related force. And reporting from Popular Information exposed a Senate Republican dark-money group operating a network of fake local news sites in competitive states, including a demonstrably false attack ad against Senator Jon Ossoff that had already reached 78 million impressions.

Taken as a whole, the week traced a recognizable pattern: executive assertion met by institutional resistance, followed in some cases by retreat and in others by renewed defiance. The Supreme Court's rejection of the original birthright citizenship order did not end the effort to restrict it; it simply prompted a reformulated one. The standoff over the Justice Department's slush fund did not disappear—it was traded away to secure a confirmation vote. Courts continued to serve as the most consistent check on executive overreach, ruling against the administration in the overwhelming majority of First Amendment cases and blocking unilateral action on tariffs, voter rolls, and the White House grounds itself. Yet enforcement agencies continued to expand their reach into airports, hospitals, and military families' lives, often with diminishing transparency about the consequences. And twice during the week, voters in Missouri and Kansas demonstrated that constitutional guardrails built to resist concentrated power still retain their own kind of durability—proof that the contest over how authority is exercised in American life was not confined to Washington, but being decided, ballot by ballot, in the states as well. ```

Title: The Attorney General's Lawyer, a Ballroom at the Supreme Court, and Shock Gloves at the Border
Content:
```markdown This was a week in which three separate institutions bent toward the same center of gravity. The Justice Department, the federal courts handling the White House's own property disputes, and the machinery of immigration enforcement all moved, in their own ways, further from the constraints that had defined them before. By week's end, a crypto pardon, a family-linked bank charter, and a repealed anti-money-laundering rule sat alongside continued defiance of federal court orders and a rapidly expanding immigration enforcement apparatus — developments that, taken individually, might read as isolated stories, but which together describe a single week's accumulation of precedent.

**The Weekend**

The weekend began with a setback for the president. A three-judge appeals panel ruled that Trump could not build a White House ballroom without congressional approval, finding that a president is, in the court's words, a "temporary tenant" of the property he occupies. Trump called the ruling politically motivated and a national security threat, and promised to appeal — a promise that would harden into a formal Supreme Court petition before the week was out. Modest as it might sound, the ballroom dispute became one of the week's clearest tests of whether a president accepts limits on his authority over public property or simply routes around them.

That same weekend, in a 50-49 vote just before a five-week recess, the Senate confirmed Todd Blanche — Trump's former personal criminal defense attorney — as attorney general, after assurances that a disputed "anti-weaponization fund" would not go forward. The confirmation placed a man who had spent years defending Trump in court atop the federal law enforcement apparatus meant to operate independently of the president it serves. The implications would not stay theoretical for long: Trump himself offered an early preview of what an accommodating Justice Department might look like, publicly attacking U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro for dropping vandalism charges against a former Olympian and demanding she reverse the decision, despite evidence the underlying damage stemmed from faulty installation rather than vandalism.

The weekend also carried early signs of economic trouble that would recur throughout the week. The Labor Department reported a 23,000-job loss in July, with more than 100,000 in downward revisions to prior months, and polling showed inflation concern nearly doubling since 2024, from 24 percent to 36 percent of respondents. Administration officials would spend much of the following days denying this data existed, even as it appeared on-screen during interviews — insisting the economy was thriving in a pattern that ran counter to figures the public could verify. Elsewhere over the weekend, the Senate voted along party lines against a federal voter ID mandate, and ICE summoned Haitian nationals under Temporary Protected Status to an Ohio facility, fitting them with ankle monitors without advance notice — a quiet escalation that would be extended further later in the week.

**Monday**

The pace accelerated. Trump signed Executive Order 14420, substantially rewriting the childhood vaccine schedule: splitting the MMR vaccine into three separate shots, reducing the number of universally recommended childhood vaccines from 18 to 11 diseases, and directing the Attorney General to challenge state vaccine mandates. Trump and HHS Secretary Robert Kennedy repeatedly invoked a discredited link between vaccines and autism in defending the order. Whatever its legal durability, the order moved federal health policy decisively away from CDC guidance and toward claims the scientific community has rejected, with public health consequences that would unfold over a longer horizon than this single week.

The same day, the Justice Department announced a program offering cities up to $300 million in policing grants in exchange for adopting federal immigration enforcement and anti-homelessness policies and agreeing to reimburse future federal deployments; several Democratic-led cities declined to apply, rejecting the conditions attached to the money. DHS, meanwhile, published procurement plans to spend up to $20 million on electric-shock "G.L.O.V.E." devices for ICE agents, despite manufacturer warnings against their use on vulnerable populations — a significant escalation in the force capability available to an agency already facing criticism over its tactics. And in North Carolina, the Republican-controlled legislature passed a bill allowing the state Supreme Court's GOP majority to remove judges without independent recommendation, building on a documented pattern of selectively pursuing ethics complaints against Democratic justices while excusing comparable conduct by Republicans.

Monday's developments connected directly to the attorney general's confirmation two days earlier. The Justice Department issued a memo broadening executive privilege to cover communications with any outside adviser the president consults — a change that would let the White House resist congressional subpoenas aimed at private citizens and companies, potentially blunting a future opposition Congress's oversight power. The department also sued New York, Connecticut, and Vermont over in-state tuition policies for undocumented students, while separate reporting revealed that more than $323 million had been redirected from National Park Service funding toward White House grounds projects — a nearly 5,000 percent increase since 2024.

**Tuesday**

Tuesday extended the immigration enforcement theme into the realm of political speech. The State Department revoked more than 175,000 visas, including over 100 from parents suspected of seeking birthright citizenship for their children, and others targeting individuals for political commentary, such as a Turkish student who had criticized her university's position on Gaza. The scale and apparent purpose of the revocations — reaching into constitutional birthright citizenship questions and punishing speech — marked a significant expansion of immigration authority as an instrument against dissent.

The same day, a watchdog analysis found that Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito had gained up to $2.9 million from oil and gas holdings he had not disclosed, prompting calls for recusal as the Court prepared to hear a climate-liability case involving the same industry; both Alito and the Court rejected the calls. Blanche was formally sworn in as attorney general that day as well, in a ceremony closed to the press but attended by FBI Director Kash Patel, administered by a former Trump defense lawyer turned federal judge. A retired conservative judge described Blanche as "the symbol of Donald Trump's corruption of the rule of law." Separately, José Mejía Hernández suffered a brain bleed and traumatic injury during an ICE arrest in Arlington, Virginia; DHS said he had tried to flee, while his lawyers alleged excessive and unjustified force.

**Wednesday**

Wednesday brought a lawsuit testing the boundaries of presidential self-dealing. Intercept Media and the Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Trump over "Truth API," a subscription service charging up to $100,000 per month for early access to presidential posts announcing official government business, alleging First and Fifth Amendment violations. The same day, the Justice Department arrested Heidi Beirich, a prominent researcher of far-right extremism, on financial crime charges connected to a broader case against the Southern Poverty Law Center — an arrest her attorney characterized as politically motivated retaliation. The Treasury Department and FinCEN eliminated the requirement that companies report beneficial ownership information, a rule enacted in 2020 to curb money laundering, and ordered the deletion of data already collected under it. And press secretary Karoline Leavitt announced she would step down by the end of August, closing a twenty-month tenure marked by attempts to control press access, the blocking of the Associated Press, and a documented pattern of falsehoods from the White House podium.

**Thursday**

Thursday was the week's densest day. HHS finalized a rule eliminating Medicaid and CHIP funding for gender-affirming care for transgender youth, effective October 13, despite nearly 90 percent of the 35,000 public comments received opposing the change. A federal judge dismissed the administration's lawsuit alleging Harvard had failed to protect Jewish students, finding the government had not plausibly shown an ongoing civil rights violation — a rare judicial check on the administration's use of litigation to pressure university compliance. The Trump-allied Kennedy Center board, separately, voted to inscribe Trump's name on the building and proceed with a renovation closure plan, directly defying a May federal court ruling that only Congress could rename the venue — an open act of institutional defiance distinct from, but structurally similar to, the ballroom fight playing out in parallel.

The financial threads converged sharply that day as well. Trump pardoned Binance founder Changpeng Zhao, who had pleaded guilty to anti-money-laundering violations, while new reporting detailed roughly $2.2 billion in personal revenue accrued during his presidency through crypto ventures, a $10 billion IRS settlement, and a $400 million plane gift from Qatar. Trump also signed a proclamation imposing tariffs of up to 100 percent on unmanned aircraft systems, invoking Section 232 national security authority to bypass ordinary trade negotiation. And court documents revealed a federal surveillance operation — "Operation Puppet Master" — that had infiltrated meetings and surveilled progressive organizations and labor unions in Minnesota following a killing by federal agents, with fifteen people ultimately charged.

**Friday**

By Friday, the week's major threads arrived at once. The administration formally petitioned the Supreme Court to stay the appeals court order halting White House ballroom construction, arguing the injunction threatened presidential security, with the lower ruling otherwise set to take effect August 21 — completing the arc from appeals court loss to direct Supreme Court confrontation. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted conditional approval for a bank charter to World Liberty Financial Trust Company, a crypto venture roughly 38 percent owned by Trump and his family, allowing it to issue a Trump-backed stablecoin under a regulator operating within his own administration. The Justice Department again refused a judge's order to release unredacted Epstein investigation documents required by statute, while it was separately confirmed that Blanche, as acting attorney general, had approved a second indictment of James Comey and reauthorized firing squad executions. And ICE and TSA began coordinating airport arrests of individuals with expired visas, including legally employed workers, while DHS extended mandatory ankle monitoring to Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio without public explanation — prompting Senator Angus King to ask publicly whether the agency's shock-glove plans reflected de-escalation or intimidation. Retail sales, meanwhile, fell 0.6 percent against a forecast increase, closing out a week of economic data that consistently undercut official messaging.

Viewed end to end, the week records less a single event than the compounding of several ongoing tests: whether a Justice Department led by the president's own former lawyer can act independently of him; whether courts retain the practical power to constrain presidential decisions about public property once a president decides to appeal past them; and whether financial entanglement between a president's family and the regulators meant to oversee them carries any institutional cost. None of these questions were resolved this week. But the distance each covered — from an appeals court ruling to a Supreme Court petition, from a judge's order to a board's open defiance, from a pardoned crypto founder to a bank charter for the president's own family business — was measured in days, not years, and the record of that pace is itself part of what the week leaves behind. ```
Excerpt: This week was defined by the completion of one long-building story and the acceleration of several others.

Title: The Week the Guardrails Were Tested — and Mostly Held
Content:
```markdown The week began with a blunt admission. Attorney General Todd Blanche, appearing on NBC's Meet the Press shortly after his confirmation, told interviewer Kristen Welker that "no attorney general should ever pledge" independence from the president. It was a small sentence with large implications, and it echoed through the days that followed, as the Justice Department kept pressing states for voter roll data it had already lost in court twenty-two times, and as prosecutors prepared to defend one of the more peculiar cases in recent memory: a charge against former FBI Director James Comey over an Instagram photo of seashells arranged to spell "8647."

That same weekend, immigration enforcement intensified in ways that stretched due process past its usual limits. ICE agents began arresting people inside courthouses, the same practice a judge had already found created a chilling effect on anyone seeking legal recourse. Newly appointed immigration judges—some explicitly cast as "deportation judges"—ran mass hearings with as little as fifteen days' notice, generating tens of thousands of in-absentia removal orders for people who never had a real chance to appear. A Texas Tribune investigation added another data point: children held in detention well past the twenty-day legal limit. Taken together, the weekend's immigration news described a system optimized for speed and volume, with notice and hearing rights treated as obstacles rather than safeguards.

Financial self-dealing surfaced too. Late Friday, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted a preliminary bank charter to World Liberty Financial, a crypto venture tied to the Trump and Witkoff families that has already funneled more than $1.6 billion to them; Trump himself had personally made close to $600 million selling stablecoins through the venture. A federal regulator, appointed by the president, had just approved a banking charter enriching the president's own family—a transaction that would later prompt Senator Elizabeth Warren to introduce legislation barring presidents from owning banks. Alongside this, Trump staged a photo-op crediting himself for a drug-price drop that had actually resulted from Biden-era Medicare negotiations, claimed inflation was falling, asserted the U.S. controlled the Strait of Hormuz, and posted a long list of exaggerated statistics on crime and prices. He also found time to redirect military engineering: a new national security memorandum ordered the Navy to revert to older steam catapults on aircraft carriers, and he floated redesigning the carrier command island and adding golden seals to the White House ballroom—personal taste overriding professional judgment on hardware meant to last decades.

By Monday, the Supreme Court delivered a piece of news that cut the other way. The justices rejected Trump's petition for rehearing in the E. Jean Carroll case, leaving the $5 million jury verdict against him intact despite his repeated efforts to undo it. It was a reminder that at least one court remained unmoved by presidential pressure on a matter already settled by a jury.

The press freedom story, which would run through much of the week, opened that same day. ABC filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC, accusing Chair Brendan Carr of demanding early license renewal for its eight stations in retaliation for editorial decisions Trump disliked, including coverage involving Jimmy Kimmel. Monday also brought a sharper, more personal confrontation: at a Georgia rally, Senator Jon Ossoff criticized Trump's reliance on aide Natalie Harp and his handling of military matters. The White House answered not with substance but with insults—communications director Steve Cheung responded crudely, and when a CNN reporter asked Trump to address Ossoff's criticism, the official White House Rapid Response account attacked the reporter directly, invoking her children. It was official government communication turned into a tool of intimidation against a journalist doing her job. Monday closed with Trump, in an Oval Office press conference, threatening to "bomb the shit out of" Oman if it interfered with reopening the Strait of Hormuz, while declaring his intent to claim the strait as U.S. territory—a statement at odds with basic principles of international law and alliance diplomacy, delivered alongside a defense of reduced military exercises with South Korea.

Tuesday deepened both threads. Disney and ABC formally filed their complaint against the FCC, this time in granular detail: more than 600 document requests, 13,000 pages of demands, and allegations of a chilling effect reaching even entertainment programming like The View. The Pentagon, separately, ordered thirty universities—including Harvard, MIT, and Johns Hopkins—to terminate foreign academic partnerships within two weeks or risk losing federal funding, a move that used financial leverage to reach into questions of academic judgment normally left to the institutions themselves. Internationally, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced sanctions against the president and a senior prosecutor of the International Criminal Court over its Gaza investigations, saying the goal was to "disable" the court's operations. And in a story that received less immediate attention but carried long-term weight, Christian nationalist figures with influence in the administration floated repealing the Nineteenth Amendment in favor of household voting arrangements in which women would defer to men at the ballot box—a proposal, not formal policy, but one voiced by people with real proximity to power.

Wednesday was quieter by comparison. The national debt passed $40 trillion, with interest payments now exceeding the defense budget, a fiscal marker that would connect later in the week to rising consumer costs. Rhode Island's governor ordered a statewide pause on new license plate readers pending a sixty-day privacy review, a small but notable instance of state government responsiveness to surveillance concerns. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's six-episode YouTube series, filmed over seven months of his tenure, premiered to just over 5,000 views—an odd footnote about how cabinet officials were spending their time and the department's platforms. And the Ossoff feud continued on cable news, with the senator defending his earlier remarks about Natalie Harp, a sign that the personal clash from Monday had not faded.

Thursday brought the week's most consequential cluster of developments. Chief Justice John Roberts stayed a lower court order that had halted construction of Trump's 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom, a project already 65 percent complete and expected to cost more than $400 million. A federal appeals court had found the project likely required congressional approval, but the stay allowed work to continue while that question remains under review—a procedural pause, not a final resolution, though one that let a disputed exercise of executive authority over public property keep moving forward in the meantime. The same day, documents obtained through FOIA litigation showed FCC Chair Brendan Carr had been in direct communication with White House officials and Sinclair Broadcast Group while overseeing the very license decisions ABC was now suing over—evidence that strengthened the broadcaster's claim that its regulator was acting as a political instrument rather than a neutral arbiter. The Justice Department, meanwhile, argued in court that Comey's seashell Instagram post could reasonably be read as a threat against the president, defending a prosecution his lawyers call vindictive and unconstitutional—a case that traced directly back to Blanche's weekend remarks about loyalty over independence. And at the Pentagon, Spokesman John Ullyot resigned after three months, criticizing Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for involving his wife in sensitive official duties; Senator Chris Coons, from the other party, separately called the arrangement "not normal," a rare moment of bipartisan unease over how classified information was being handled at the department's senior levels. Thursday closed with more evidence of the presidency blending with private commerce: a donor-funded White House renovation tour, and continued sales of early access to Trump's Truth Social posts for as much as $100,000 a month.

Friday arrived with a cluster of institutional course corrections alongside new instances of pressure on the press. The Pentagon fired the publisher, editor, and a reporter at Stars and Stripes, the military-funded news outlet, after it reported on poor conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln—conditions Trump had separately dismissed as "fake news." The firings were a distinct mechanism from the ABC/FCC lawsuit: not regulatory pressure on a private broadcaster, but direct personnel retaliation inside a military-run newsroom, aimed at journalists covering the welfare of service members. On the accountability side, the Department of Homeland Security walked back a sweeping claim it had made about noncitizen voting in Nevada. After meeting with state officials, DHS acknowledged it could confirm only 185 noncitizens on Nevada's voter rolls, a steep retreat from an earlier claimed figure of nearly 16,000, and part of a broader assertion of 278,000 such registrations across four states that had never been substantiated. It was a specific, checkable claim that collapsed on contact with actual data.

The courts, too, did not move in a single direction. A federal appeals court upheld protections limiting immigration enforcement at houses of worship, a clear check on enforcement overreach. But a federal judge also ruled that a Defense Production Act order allowed a disputed California oil pipeline to keep operating over the state's objections, and the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel concluded the Constitution requires presidential control over the Foreign Service Grievance Board—two rulings that, in different ways, validated expansive federal authority over state and institutional prerogatives. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent formally eliminated beneficial-ownership disclosure requirements for shell companies, completing a rollback that began earlier when FinCEN dismantled and destroyed the underlying registry—removing a congressionally mandated anti-corruption tool with little public notice. And the week's economic pressures became more tangible: gasoline hit $4.11 a gallon, school lunch costs rose 11 percent, and a more-than-40-percent cut to food safety inspection funding was linked to the largest cyclospora outbreak in U.S. history. Asked about the terms of a new beef trade deal, Trump told reporters simply, "I don't want to say," closing the week with a small but telling refusal of disclosure.

Seen as a whole, the week showed executive power testing its limits on several fronts at once—legal, financial, military, and rhetorical—while the institutions meant to check that power produced a mixed but not uniformly deferential record. A jury's verdict against the president stood. A regulator's coordination with the White House came to light through litigation, not official transparency. A specific, inflated claim about voter fraud fell apart once state officials asked for evidence. Journalists at a Pentagon-funded outlet lost their jobs for reporting facts the administration found inconvenient, even as a different broadcaster pressed its own case through the federal courts. None of these outcomes was final; the ballroom project proceeds under a stay, not a verdict, and the ABC/FCC lawsuit remains unresolved. But the pattern of the week was legible: pressure applied broadly and often successfully, met by scattered, real, and sometimes effective resistance from courts, state officials, and local governments unwilling to simply accept the administration's claims at face value. ```
